Breaking: Is This Department Stores’ Massive Comeback Christmas?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gone are the days of the branded luxury Christmas window.
  • In an era where department stores need to work harder than ever to get a holiday shopper into their store — rather than them shopping online, directly with a brand, or at the department store up the road — many retailers are branching out beyond the monobrand Christmas window strategy that’s dominated recent holiday seasons.
  • Last week, stores from Bergdorf Goodman to Bloomingdale’s made a splash with their holiday window unveilings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gone are the days of the branded luxury Christmas window.

In an era where department stores need to work harder than ever to get a holiday shopper into their store — rather than them shopping online, directly with a brand, or at the department store up the road — many retailers are branching out beyond the monobrand Christmas window strategy that’s dominated recent holiday seasons.

Last week, stores from Bergdorf Goodman to Bloomingdale’s made a splash with their holiday window unveilings. Saks followed suit on Monday, November 23. The weather was unseasonably warm, with attendees clad in light jackets, rather than the usual fur and puffers for this time of year. Bergdorf made up for the tepid temps with fake snow. Bloomingdale’s had Sienna Spiro sing a rendition of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas”.

In a recent development, by going the multibrand route, stores can put themselves at the center of their holiday storytelling, and appeal to a wider range of consumers by displaying merchandise across a host of different price points. Utilizing existing merchandise is also a lower lift than the logistical and financial burden of staging a full brand takeover. “I’m anticipating highly creative windows with a variety of merchandise. The general sentiment as of the last several months is that the customer shops high and low, where two years ago it was all about the substantial labels,” states luxury consultant Robert Burke. “So I think you’re going to see a variety of merchandise displayed in creative ways.”.

It’s panning out. Nordstrom is partnering with David Bowie’s estate to celebrate what would be the star’s 80th birthday — and is Nordstrom’s 125th anniversary. Included in Bowie80 are collaborations with designers including Paul Smith, Marc Jacobs and Undercover’s Jun Takahashi. Bergdorf Goodman’s windows are a vignette inspired by a Fresh York winter, celebrating 125 years with an array of capsules from brands including Michael Kors, Brunello Cucinelli and Valentino. Saks’s windows offer up a tour of the festive period in the city. Over in London, Liberty is leaning into storytelling around holiday rituals and routines, and Selfridges is, like its peers, celebrating wintertime in the city (New York City, that is).

Bergdorf invited a host of designers to participate in its holiday window unveiling.

Not all of the players are going wide, though. Bloomingdale’s Friday window unveiling was in partnership with Ralph Lauren. Partnering with Ralph was a no-brainer, says Kevin Harter, VP of integrated marketing. “Ralph Lauren is synonymous with the traditions, nostalgia and timelessness that makes the holidays so special,” she says. The evening included a festive Ralph cocktail in the store — with teddy bear sweaters aplenty — and David Lauren was onstage to celebrate the unveiling alongside Bloomingdale’s CEO Olivier Bron. Inside, though, there are an array of brand activations — over 50 — from Barbour’s Tea & Sympathy pop-up to Ugg’s takeover of the Bloomingdale’s restaurant — and famed froyo destination — Forty Carrots. (There’s an Ugg-exclusive flavor, of course.) Ralph Lauren is the anchor, Harter says.

It has been revealed that overall, this multibrand, amped-up storytelling logic extends to the in-store experience itself. Department stores this season have built out their holiday strategies around curation, with the view of inspiring their customers with the creative while making their lives as easy as possible. “One of the biggest opportunities for retail at Christmas is getting the balance between inspiration and ease right,” says Lydia King, managing director of retail at Liberty.

This is especially important this year, after department stores weathered quieter holiday seasons amid the upheaval of recent years. 2026 started with a bang, as Saks Global declared bankruptcy in January and, since summer, has been pushing its comeback as Exemplar Luxury Group. Bloomingdale’s, too, has spent 2026 pushing upmarket, making the most of a moment in which many of its contemporaries are struggling to meet the moment. This festive period, the stakes are high, capping off a year in which US department stores sought to regain lost magic.

Here’s how department stores are meeting the moment for this all-key holiday season.

Recent findings suggest that this season, retailers are placing emphasis on their curation for the holiday period. The single-brand focus made sense a few years back when luxury was at its peak, Burke indicates. But now, he argues, department stores are looking to be more democratic in price point and product. “Compared to a few years ago, I’m seeing a lot of interest in smaller brands and independent brands,” he says. “The luxury customer today, even at the highest level, their mindset is very open to not having to only have major luxury branded merchandise.”.

Department stores are curating more than just product, though. Across the board — and in keeping with Gen Z’s desire for shopping experiences that offer meaning and excitement inaccessible via social media — they’re placing emphasis on the unique experiences offered in-store throughout the holidays.

Nordstrom’s holiday facade is an embrace of Bowie.

In doing so, they’re putting themselves at the center of the narrative. Bergdorf Goodman is doing this literally, placing the store in the middle of its New York-themed holiday campaign and window display which, this year, literally leads shoppers inside. “After the sidewalk introduces you to the narrative, it continues through the main doors into a Zhivago-esque wintry snow-laden forest hung with rock crystal chandeliers and a flock of white geese overhead,” notes Linda Fargo, SVP of Bergdorf’s fashion office and store presentation.

Recent findings suggest that “This year we’ve put much more emphasis on the whole experience of Christmas at Liberty, beyond the product offering,” notes Liberty’s King. The store’s campaign, The Liberty Christmas Chronicles, follows the rituals of the season — preparing, dressing, traveling, gathering, unwinding and eventually resting — with gifting running throughout, of course. “We know customers increasingly value curation, personalization and expertise,” she says.

This comes in via mini in-store experiences, from wreath-making with Diptyque (Liberty’s hero partner in its Atrium section) to build-your-own hampers in the Liberty Food Hall. Other activations include personalized bows with Moët & Chandon, lipstick engraving with Lisa Eldridge and makeup bag embroidery with Westman Atelier.

According to recent reports, selfridges is taking a similar multibrand approach with tailored, ‘only available here’ experiences. With Canada Goose on Duke Street, for instance, the retailer has constructed an Arctic-inspired research outpost with hot chocolates and personalized luggage tags, and the ultra-buzzy Vice City GTA VI pop-up kicked off the retailer’s holiday activities.

“These partnerships help create a Christmas that feels distinctive to Selfridges,” states marketing and experiences director Rebecca Warburton. “We know that people are looking for experiences, opportunities to connect with others and to create memorable moments,” she says, noting that Selfridges looked to offer more reasons for customers to spend time at the store this season.

Saks is leaning into these in-person experiences more than ever. For the first time, L’Avenue at Saks will host breakfast with Santa throughout the season and will transform into Le Chalet, with festive menu programming, on holiday season weekends.

Sienna Spiro performed at the Bloomingdale’s x Ralph Lauren window unveiling.

Industry observers note that this curation extends to stores’ gifting options. Beyond offering a smart selection of brands, stores are also thinking more deeply about their non-fashion gifting options, so that customers will shop with them not just for shoes, but for stocking stuffers, too.

It has been revealed that bergdorf Goodman does this well, Burke notes, noting the store’s “tremendous” holiday season in 2025. “Bergdorf’s home floor is a very good example of it being a tourist destination with fun Christmas merchandise, because they sell all of these Christmas ornaments, candies and candles. It takes over the entire seventh floor,” he says. In celebration of its 125th anniversary, Bergdorf is upping the ante this year with an Assouline legacy book, Very Bergdorf, ‘Very Bergdorf’ specialty ornaments, plus a snow globe featuring the Bergdorf Goodman facade. “Every part of the store has something uniquely made for us, and it all adds up to a very Bergdorf holiday,” Fargo says.

Industry observers note that this year, Nordstrom is partnering with toy companies including FAO Schwarz and Jellycats. “You think about a retailer being relevant and having all the things customers want to buy — particularly at the holidays — partnerships like that help, in addition to carrying the best brands in the world,” states Deniz Anders, EVP, chief marketing officer. “Being able to check off their list for everyone across the family, that’s something that we’re really focused on.” Nordstrom has also invested more in consumables this year, and has a partnership with fashion-favorite Flamingo Estate.

In a recent development, this season, department stores are thinking more than ever about ease. Saving customers time and effort, execs believe, is the way to capture their hearts — and their spend.

Industry observers note that nordstrom has expanded its gift shops in common areas throughout the store. “It’s really not something that we used to do, but we want customers to know this is a place that you can buy gifts at broad price points,” Anders states. The retailer tested the cross-store setup last year and has expanded the size of the shops this season. “We want to make it easy and fun for customers to buy gifts.”.

Liberty’s largest holiday season development is the introduction of its Gifting Curator service, King indicates. “For the first time, customers can book one-to-one appointments with Liberty experts who can guide them across the whole store, rather than within a single category or brand,” she says. “The idea is to make discovering the right present feel as special as giving it.” To round out the experience, Liberty has introduced a gift-wrapping experience with wrapper Roxy Wraps.

Stores have also been planting seeds to get their customers in the shopping mindset. Though all of the substantial, splashy window displays were unveiled at their usual time, just before Thanksgiving, the communications around the holiday season started far earlier. Nordstrom sent out its holiday catalog a week earlier than usual, Anders says. It’s the retailer’s biggest catalog ever. “We’ve been bringing in gifts a lot earlier,” she says. “Holiday is a marathon and you’ve got to have the gifts early and be ready to serve customers and bring a little joy and fun.”.

The allure of soft, understated nails is going nowhere. In preparation for party season, expect to see minuscule flecks of metallic gold and star-themed motifs, too. While milky pink nails will always be in style, this winter, it’s all about unexpected sheers like lavender, bronze, and pearly white. Not only do these colors go with everything, but they also are extremely forgiving—you can paint them on yourself without a problem.

Zoya Lavender Perfector Nail Polish.

Londontown Illuminating Nail Concealer in Bare.

Essie Gel Couture Long-Lasting Nail Polish in Liquid Diamonds.

Below, find 10 of the most polished, pared-back nail ideas to bookmark for your next appointment.

Last season, we had Hailey Bieber milk nails, followed by Sienna Miller’s ‘Chantilly cream’. Now? Lavender takes the spotlight, in its dreamiest, near-translucent form. A high-shine top coat makes this tone appear even hazier in the light.

It has been revealed that leaning into minimalism doesn’t necessarily mean forgoing color. Take this rich, berry red for proof; when an all-over pigment isn’t on the cards, a sleek micro French tip is equally flattering.

It has been revealed that for a simpler take on autumn’s ‘gold fairy dust’ nail trend (as seen on Taylor Swift), draw inspiration from stardust instead. Here, a natural blushed pink base sits beautifully under a gently dazzling, golden shimmer top coat.

It has been revealed that traditional French tips are given a modern, metallic upgrade without veering into futuristic territory. When reserved for the base of the nail, a gold-toned cuff is eye-catching but in a subtle way.

Frosted pearlescent finishes are as luminous as they are delicate—not to mention destined for winter weather. When worn with a cozy cashmere knit, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more perfect pairing.

Recent findings suggest that square and squoval nails are seeing a revival this season. Keep your shapes cropped, softly rounded, and ultra-glossy if committing to minimalism.

It has been revealed that trade in winter's deep, vibrant mocha, espresso, and cocoa-inspired browns for a sheer bronze pigment. When kept close to the natural nail color, this shade is the best way to embrace elevated color without going overboard.

While the notion of nail art might suggest something elaborate colorful, petite star motifs make a case for the opposite. One on each nail balances a feeling of festivity with practicality for everyday wear.

In a recent development, granted, a white Christmas might be far on the horizon. But this set sees micro polka dots get a dainty, wintry upgrade, inspired by tiny droplets of snow.

Sources indicate that if a micro French isn’t your style, an ombré is worth considering. Begin with a nude beige-pink base color, and watch it blend seamlessly into a cozy, seasonal color.

#100522. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (414 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior.
  • More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.
  • Sources indicate that preheat oven to 425°.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Sources indicate that preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Recent findings suggest that combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The holidays are a time for families to come together, but for Guy Fieri, they’re also a reminder of the loved ones no longer with us.
  • The chef and television personality posted a photo of himself and his late father, Jim, on Instagram to commemorate what would have been his 84th birthday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holidays are a time for families to come together, but for Guy Fieri, they’re also a reminder of the loved ones no longer with us.

The chef and television personality posted a photo of himself and his late father, Jim, on Instagram to commemorate what would have been his 84th birthday. It’s been nearly three years since his father passed away following a long battle with pancreatic cancer.

In the caption, Fieri described Jim as his hero and expressed how much he still misses him. Fans quickly filled the comments with condolences and support.

According to recent reports, “Sending love on this special day,” one user wrote. On Facebook, another commented, “I hope your memories of your dad comfort you today. He must have been so proud of you.”.

Industry observers note that others shared their own happy memories of Jim. “I miss the stories and conversations with this man,” one person wrote. “He was the best!!” Another recalled, “Jim was a true romantic. I'll never forget when he made the rose petal trail for your mom.”.

In a recent development, fieri has been open about how deeply the loss affected him. “I wanna call him all the time and ask questions, help me solve complications or celebrate the wins,” he mentioned in a series of Instagram Stories last year. “Wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for him and it's hard to be here without him.”.

It has been revealed that birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays are still hard for Fieri, but he’s also found some comfort in his family. In a 2024 interview with Graham Bensinger, he said, “The funny thing is, out of everything that's happened, it has made me probably 10 times closer to my mom.”.

Inside Fashion’s $276 Billion Succession Shakeup

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What appears to be a succession story at a handful of prominent luxury companies is, in fact, a defining moment for the wider industry, with the potential to reshape fashion’s competitive map, a new report says.
  • “Succession is one of the 10 themes that we believe will shape fashion in the next decade,” notes the report’s author, Achim Berg, who in 2025 created FashionSights, a research and advisory boutique, after 23 years at McKinsey.
  • Industry observers note that the report “Fashion’s Succession Problem: The Generational Transfer Reshaping the Industry” is an excerpt from a book Berg co-wrote with Paula Trus titled The Future of Fashion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What appears to be a succession story at a handful of prominent luxury companies is, in fact, a defining moment for the wider industry, with the potential to reshape fashion’s competitive map, a new report says.

“Succession is one of the 10 themes that we believe will shape fashion in the next decade,” notes the report’s author, Achim Berg, who in 2025 created FashionSights, a research and advisory boutique, after 23 years at McKinsey.

Industry observers note that the report “Fashion’s Succession Problem: The Generational Transfer Reshaping the Industry” is an excerpt from a book Berg co-wrote with Paula Trus titled The Future of Fashion. It is set for publication in March by Bocconi University Press. Ahead of its release, Berg shares the report’s key findings with Vogue Business.

Vogue: Why is succession a defining theme of the next decade?

In a recent development, achim Berg: We built our index while writing the book. It’s called FashionSights Global 100 (FSG100), a database of the world’s 100 largest fashion and apparel companies ranked by revenue. Out of 100 companies, 46 are family-owned. And out of the 46 companies with family dominance, two-thirds (or 30 companies) face a succession challenge, according to our analysis. These 30 companies generated a combined $276 billion in revenues in 2025. The main criteria for companies meeting what we call succession risk is that they are led by the first or second generation, and those who are in charge, which could be advisory, supervisory board or management, are 65 or older. We also added companies that have publicly acknowledged a succession challenge. It’s worth noting that 63% of the companies navigating succession challenges are based in Europe, 30% in North America and the remaining 7% in Asia-Pacific.

Why is this great generational transfer now?

In a recent development, most of those companies that are around now, with a few exceptions, were founded in the ’60s, ’70s, ’80s, or ’90s of the last century. Ralph Lauren sold his first ties in 1967. In 1975, Amancio Ortega opened his first Zara store. And in 1984, Tadashi Yanai opened the first Uniqlo store. Modern fashion retail is 60 years old.

How do you define family dominance?

Recent findings suggest that either the family has more than 50% share capital, or more than 50% of the voting rights. But also, in some cases, they do not even need to have that much because they are still the biggest shareholders and they call the shots. Some families have special voting rights or legal structures that allow them to play a larger role.

What are some of the ways succession will play out for these companies?

Industry observers note that it depends. First, will the departing owner hand over on time? And second, are the heirs as capable as the founders? Succession will occupy a lot of time and energy, and that could derail some of those businesses. Some of that trouble will lead them to M&A in whatever shape and form. Generational handover could accelerate consolidation as families consider partnerships, outside investment or a sale. We’re only looking at 30 of the largest 100 companies. But you will also find many smaller businesses facing similar succession challenges and looking to sell. It’s not a given that they’re all going to find an acquirer.

Sources indicate that when it comes to buyers, established fashion groups could gain scale through acquisitions and expand their portfolios with newly introduced brands. We notably see opportunities for stronger Italian luxury groups.

According to recent reports, we also see opportunities for new owners from the beauty and eyewear industries. Think about L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica and the discussion around Armani. They were considered suitable acquirers by Mr Armani himself. It could also be a good opportunity for those companies to become more relevant in the fashion space.

In a recent development, last but not least, brand ownership and licensing companies such as ABG, WHP Global and Marquee Brands could offer another route for families seeking an exit. I interviewed [ABG founder and executive chairman] Jamie Salter for my book. He claims publicly that his ecosystem generates $38 billion in annual retail sales by now. So they can do massive acquisitions globally, and they’re looking for global brands to create licensing.

Some successions, however, are expected to proceed smoothly, according to the report.

Sources indicate that yes, the report identifies clear responsibilities, independent oversight and successors tested through meaningful experience as a foundation for successful handovers. In the white paper, you will see that we consider the handover at Zegna as one of those more positive examples. Gildo Zegna is the group executive chair. Gianluca Tagliabue is the group CEO. And Gildo Zegna’s two sons, Edoardo and Angelo Zegna, are also now playing a role as co-CEOs of the Zegna brand and are groomed for succession. A succession typically takes 10 to 15 years of preparation, and our observation is that many of the businesses need to seriously engage in those preparations.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that known for its sprawling campus and sun-soaked galleries filled with modernist and contemporary masterpieces, the Art Institute of Chicago in Grant Park remains one of the oldest and largest art museums in the world, dating all the way back to 1879.
  • No visit to Chicago is complete without enjoying some jazz.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chicago is a great place to be year-round (yes, even in the dead of winter). And it doesn’t hurt that there’s always plenty to see and do. Spend the day at the Art Institute of Chicago, grab a deep-dish pizza at Pequod’s, or simply explore the city and see where the day takes you. If you’re planning to be in town this weekend or over the holidays, Chi-town is ripe for a visit—or even a staycation. Whether you’re heading to the Windy City for the art, the food, or a future music festival, consider this your nonexhaustive guide to what to see, where to eat, and everything in between.

Recent findings suggest that known for its sprawling campus and sun-soaked galleries filled with modernist and contemporary masterpieces, the Art Institute of Chicago in Grant Park remains one of the oldest and largest art museums in the world, dating all the way back to 1879. The permanent collections are exceptional, but the Institute’s heavy rotation of standout exhibitions makes it worth the visit.

No visit to Chicago is complete without enjoying some jazz. Situated in Chicago’s Uptown neighborhood, the iconic century-old Green Mill plays host to live music seven days a week, with Thursday nights specifically dedicated to swing dancing and the third Sunday of every month to poetry slams. This famed, cash-only entertainment venue was a local haunt of mobster Al Capone, who frequented the establishment during Prohibition. Patrons can still sit in his booth, which has a clear view of both exits (for obvious reasons).

It has been revealed that get lost among the Spanish Baroque-style structures capped with gold rotundas, lagoons, and more, before arriving at the stunning glass greenhouse that ensconces the Garfield Park Conservatory. Traverse through the manicured gardens and wander between themed rooms with spaces dedicated to palms, ferns, desert cacti, succulents, and exotic flora (why not?). Throughout the year, the Conservatory hosts special pop-up events like beer tastings, yoga, expert talks, and, yes, flower shows.

Guest In Residence Grizzly Jacket.

Top Chef winner and South Side native Joe Flamm brings Italian-Croatian flavor to the West Loop’s Fulton Market district with his restaurant Rose Mary. The buzzy concept offers a modern take on rustic dishes, packed with bold flavors and thoughtful coursing that encapsulates what Flamm has coined “Adriatic drinking food.” The open kitchen gives dining patrons a glimpse of all the action, and amid exacting sous chefs, you’ll sometimes see chef Joe himself calling the shots. While the menu changes seasonally, the Stracciatella starter is a must, and you can’t go wrong with the Mafaldine or Pork Ribs Pampanella.

Lincoln Park’s crown jewel, Alinea, is renowned for its ingenious molecular gastronomy, led by creative chef Grant Achatz, who has earned the eatery three Michelin stars and a bevy of awards. Enter through an unmarked door and enjoy a multi-course tasting menu with inventive creations like a single-bite black truffle explosion or a complex take on surf and turf with nuanced flavors plated with surgical precision, and a dessert finale that looks like a literal splatter of paint right on your dining table. The Alinea experience comes complete with scented vapors, tricks, and tableside theatrics, so you’ll be plenty entertained throughout.

Industry observers note that if you want the ultimate deep-dish experience, Pequod’s reigns supreme. It’s been an institution since the ’70s and an undisputed choice among locals for traditional pan pizza (hold for those who will try to keep this a secret from out-of-towners). What sets Pequod’s apart from other deep-dish joints is the crunchy, caramelized crust that some will say is a transcendent experience, making it the best pizza in Chicago, if not one of the best in the country.

Recent findings suggest that where better to enjoy a martini than under 24-karat gold Tiffany & Co. candelabras and Grecian frescos by French painter Louis Pierre Rigal? Palmer House is opulence defined—a hotel packed with history and enduring romantic myths that swirl around its origins. Enter the lobby through the travertine double staircase and you’re immediately transported to another universe. The French-inspired aesthetic can trace its roots back to Bertha Palmer, the lucky dame who was gifted the hotel as an extravagant wedding gift by her husband, Potter Palmer. After befriending Claude Monet, she began amassing a remarkable amount of Impressionist art that stood as the largest collection outside of France (now on display at the Art Institute). Enjoy a cocktail at Palmer’s Lockwood Lobby Bar before starting your evening. Pro tip: Live entertainment is offered on weekends.

Tucked away in a secret alleyway entrance, Three Dots and a Dash is a whimsical take on an island bar, with exotic craft cocktails and tropical elixirs. Pick your poison by flavor, clever name, or the eccentric mug it’s housed in. For rum connoisseurs, the Bamboo Room inside offers a dedicated experience with a focused menu of daiquiris, renditions of classics, and progressive cocktails made using a modern technique.

This sprawling rooftop at the edge of Navy Pier has the best perch in town, with sweeping views of Lake Michigan and the coastal skyline. The bright and airy space is open year-round, with fire pits, game areas, and cozy seating ideal for group hangs and intimate get-togethers by day or night. And if you’re fresh to Chicago, it’s the perfect place to stop after exploring Grant Park and the Pier.

Liffner Paper Croc-Effect Leather Clutch.

Nestled on a side street near Chicago’s Water Tower Place, The Peninsula Chicago is perfect for anyone heading to the city for a shopping spree. Ralph’s Coffee is just steps away (and seems to always have a line stretching outside), and the Red Line is close for easy travel. The hotel’s amenities also stand out. The indoor pool is bathed in sunlight for picturesque laps, and the spa is top-tier. If you’re looking for a convenient bite or drink, Shanghai Terrace and Z Bar have you covered. The best part, however? The Sky Rink opens right around the holidays for a fun winter ice skate.

It has been revealed that right across the street from the famous Chicago River, The St. Regis Chicago is in the center of all the action. Navy Pier, The Art Institute of Chicago, and Grant Park are all just a short stroll away. And if you want to stay in and take advantage of all that the hotel has to offer, there are options galore. Take your pick of evening champagne socials, luxury suites that come equipped with your own private butler, or the world-class spa that offers immersive experiences like meditation and sound baths.

Located in Chicago’s iconic Loop, the Pendry Chicago is near some of the city’s most iconic architectural hits. Both Millennium Park and Grant Park are within walking distance, and the hotel is known for its commitment to wellness rituals, including its partnership with AIRE Ancient Baths, which has steam rooms and treatments—perfect for some R&R. It’s also located in the 1920s-era Carbide & Carbon Building and carries the Art Deco style throughout, making it feel like you’re living in the world of The Great Gatsby.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, anyone who’s ever been trapped on a stalled subway or a WiFi-less flight knows how screwed we might feel without access to our phones. Last week’s tech outages––first, a failure of Microsoft’s systems, then, a national grounding of flights, followed by problems from Charles Schwab to Apple iCloud––were a reminder of how fragile our digital infrastructure is, especially at the dawn of AI. Preppers on Reddit, better known for discussing generators and the storage of food, began talking about how to AI–apocalypse proof the devices we’re all so dependent on. “getting serious about my preps with all the cyber attacks going on,” one user wrote. “I work for a security organization so I get a front row seat to a lot of the chaos. I’m specifically prepping for prolonged loss of power.”.

Many found their way to Nomad, a pocket-sized device created to aid in offline situations. “I had huge, huge spikes in traffic,” stated Jackson Studner, creator of Nomad and a student at Millersville University of Pennsylvania. (“I’m not a company or a startup, just a college student who enjoys building useful things and sharing them,” Studner’s website reads.) With the help of his professors, he built Nomad to provide some entertainment on camping trips and cross-country trips with friends. They’d hit a dead zone, and realize they wanted to watch a movie, or run video game software. Nomad is a miniscule server with TV and films, the entire Wikipedia library, and portable Wi-Fi, and offline maps. “I really like the reliability aspect,” Studner tells me. “I like to own my stuff. It's kind of that simple.” He’s also added navigation for his newly introduced community preparing for the apocalypse (or at least a grid shutdown). “It will actually tell you how to go along the road, it can tell you how to walk there, it'll calculate times, that kind of stuff,” he said.

Industry observers note that elsewhere, there are emergency libraries that you can download to your existing computer, with offline chatbots that can tell you how to find clean water or start a fire: lastbook.org, which includes how-to videos; Survival LLM, which offers up information from the CDC and FEMA; and Project Nomad (different from Studner’s Nomad), from Chris Sherwood, a prominent YouTuber. Sherwood is best known for posting explainer videos showing viewers how to build their “homelabs”—personal, at-home computing devices—under the name Crosstalk Solutions.

Industry observers note that the interest in Project Nomad, Sherwood said, has been overwhelming. “It’s got over 40,000 stars on GitHub, which means that 40,000 people not only saw the project and were on the page, but they clicked the little button to favorite it. And I'm getting over 200,000 views on the website per month,” he said.

In a recent development, despite his fresh fans, Sherwood himself isn’t a prepper. He was inspired by the Information Technology Disaster Resource Center (ITDRC), a non-profit that goes into disasters and provides internet services when they are completely down. “I had the opportunity to go on deployment with [ITDRC] when Hurricane Ian came through, and I saw firsthand all these people that were offline. It was a disaster. Getting people back online was almost as notable as the food and water supplies that were getting set up to help with the recovery,” he explained.

According to recent reports, studner wasn’t a prepper either–– at first. But since Nomad took off and he’s found himself in more “prepper” corners of the internet, his feelings have slightly changed. “It’s for peace of mind. I have my little go bag. I'm not too, too worried about it, but I like to know that if there ever was a real problem, I'd be okay in that situation.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Sources indicate that remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

Meet ‘Dune: Part Three’’s Ida Brooke, the Young Brit Denis Villeneuve Picked to Play Zendaya’s Daughter

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ida Brooke is wearing a piece of Dune around her neck.
  • “There’s nothing that’s going to be as good as that,” the 18-year-old actor claims, turning it between her fingers over coffee in a central London café.
  • To get there was a months-long exercise in trying not to unravel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ida Brooke is wearing a piece of Dune around her neck. The necklace is silver and unassuming, but she explains its provenance: at the end of filming Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, silver used in the production was collected, melted down, and recast into wrap gifts for the cast. Brooke hasn’t taken hers off since.

“There’s nothing that’s going to be as good as that,” the 18-year-old actor claims, turning it between her fingers over coffee in a central London café. It has changed the rest of her jewelry too: once a gold devotee, today she is wearing a stack of silver rings. (She is otherwise dressed in the Gen-Z uniform of a tank top and low-rise cargo trousers, her hair falling in glossy natural curls.) It feels particularly apt for someone whose life is currently divided into very distinct before and afters. Only a few months ago, she was a film student at the Brit School; soon, audiences will know her as Ghanima, the daughter of Zendaya’s Chani and Timothée Chalamet’s Paul Atreides, opposite Nakoa-Wolf Momoa as her twin brother, Leto II, in Villeneuve’s third Dune film.

To get there was a months-long exercise in trying not to unravel. Brooke initially self-taped without knowing she was auditioning for Dune. When her agent revealed the project, she shut the curtains on a sunny day and watched the first two films back to back. “I fell so in love with it,” she indicates. “I was like, ‘OK, this is going to really hurt if I don’t get this.’” By the final audition, she had already convinced herself that another girl outside the room had the advantage. Brooke went to the bathroom and gave herself a talking to. “You don’t have to get it,” she remembers thinking. “You just have to show them that you have something to say. Just make their choice a little bit harder.”.

The following day, Brooke was sitting beside a teacher at school trying to solve an editing problem when a message flashed up from an unknown number: Villeneuve wanted to call her in 20 minutes. Her phone had five percent battery. She tore through the school searching for a charger, eventually hiding in a stairwell to take the call. He first warned her about the intensity of the shoot—the heat, the physical demands—and asked whether she wanted to join the film. A friend found Brooke crying and took a photograph. “She was like, ‘You might want this one day.’”.

According to recent reports, cinema has been the organizing obsession of her life since childhood. At six, she would rewatch films endlessly on a portable DVD player; as a teenager growing up in west London, she traveled across the city for Saturday acting classes. She now lives with her father and younger sibling, a household she affectionately describes as “very rowdy.” A lifelong cinephile, though he doesn’t work in film, her father’s fascination with human psychology has informed her own approach to storytelling. (The two share a love of Martin Scorsese.) “He always loved quality stories and has really good taste,” she says, smiling.

Writing interests her as much as performing: she likes structure, psychology and—gleefully—eavesdropping, listening to “the cadence of how people speak,” she claims, gesturing cheekily at the conversations trilling around us. She is currently working on a screenplay exploring Vietnam veterans and the pharmaceutical industry, a project born from the inquisitive way she approaches the world. She will also star in and executive produce an indie drama, Grass Roots, due to shoot next summer.

Calm proved instructive in the desert. Zendaya, who had already endured the elements on the earlier films, helped Brooke understand how to quiet her body enough to perform. “I feel so much more confident acting in somewhat normal environments now,” she says. Learning to act, for Brooke, has also meant learning when to pay attention and when to give in. “Denis has such a vivid imagination that you can step right into his vision… You just have to be a kid.”.

Ida Brooke as Ghanima and Nakoa-Wolf Momoa as Leto in Dune: Part Three.

Sources indicate that brooke missed her graduation—and the screening of her final Brit School film, The Operator, which won an award—because she was away filming the forthcoming sci-fi live-action Gundam movie alongside Noah Centineo and Sydney Sweeney in Australia. When she told her new castmates how gutted she was, they improvised a graduation of sorts: everyone piled onto a sofa and screened her film together. “I had that sense of community that I missed.”.

For the moment, Brooke is resisting any pressure to decide exactly what she is. Actor? Writer? Director? All three? She chose not to go to university and has instead devised her own education, meeting writers to ask how they work, reading about psychology and screenwriting, watching films, researching whatever historical period has most recently caught her imagination. “One of my biggest priorities is self-education,” she indicates.

Her necklace is a souvenir from one of the biggest film sets ever conceived, but Brooke looks voraciously forward at what she hasn’t encountered yet. She wants to work with Scorsese, but she also talks excitedly about young, unknown filmmakers in London: “The friends that I have now, I see them as my future colleagues.” Her ambition is not in conquering new terrain, it’s to remain porous enough to keep discovering. After all, silver can always be melted down and made into something new.

Industry observers note that most people might build an outfit around a pair of shoes. Others, around a jacket. But few, surprisingly, do it around a belt.

Recent findings suggest that at GQ, we’ve always said that the overlooked belt is more than the sum of its buckle and holes. Not only will it stop your slacks from going south, but a good leather belt can make just as much of a statement as your shoes, and deliver as much of a stylistic flourish as a tie. Unconvinced? Enter: The studded belt. (Which, coincidentally, we're now increasingly seeing be offered by some of the most imitated brands in the industry, from Lemaire to RRL, Mfpen to Our Legacy.).

Recent findings suggest that the charm of the studded belt is that it’s a vibe chameleon. Its decorative elements can pay tribute to any number of aesthetics, from Americana to punk to European artistry. And while any one will easily provide further flair to an already-singing outfit, the best ones also single-handedly bring even the most minimalist wardrobe to life. (And to be honest, that’s how I feel studded belts are best worn today: Against a white tee and jeans, for an easy win without changing your whole look.).

To help you find the right one for you, I've sorted through the vast waist-wear market to find a selection that won't just make your outfits sing, but set them on course for superstardom. See you out there, Stud.

Let's start gently: Somehow, Anderson’s has made a studded belt that whispers. It’s a small but mighty addition to their lovingly handcrafted Italian leather goods.

“If a stud falls out, make a wish,” is the outlook over at Htc Los Angeles—and they provide plenty of it. A true purveyor of the style, the brand has been specializing in rock-and-roll embellished leather goods since the ’90s. And they aren’t stingy with it either.

Trust Corridor NYC to come in clutch for all of your folksy Americana needs. The worn-in look of their studded belt—made in full-grain leather and tarnished hardware—carries all the tales of someone who’s worn it through the arid badlands.

If the fits over at the Ralph Lauren PoloFest in Tokyo last month have inspired you to join the RL tribe, any one of the many studded belts from RRL (Ralph's ranch-minded line) is a strong place to start.

Sources indicate that as you’ll see from our list, Our Legacy—a staple for any serious fashion guy—has secured two call-outs. Here, they cut diamond studs to form a snakeskin-like pattern that, when worn against your best corduroy pants, gives the look some severe shine.

While we’re talking about studded belts as an easy hardware win, they're also the perfect place to score some color points too. Here, the green and orange mixes it up more than traditional turquoise.

According to recent reports, since its founding in 2012, Maximum Henry has been handmaking our favorite leather goods right here in New York City, including their beloved oval buckle belt. But they also know how to do a good, uncomplicated studded belt.

Recent findings suggest that the floral studs on this OL belt aren’t merely decorative, but are punched into the very function of the eyelets. It’s a sweet look, really, and one done so effortlessly.

In a recent development, dressing for winter, when all you ever want to feel is cozy, can leave you feeling like a schlub. There is, however, an easy fix in the form of the enviably Parisian stylings of Lemaire, who’ve released a brown belt with almond-shaped studs. Wear it with your all-denim outfit or heavy grey wool pants, it’ll make you feel like one of the brand’s cityslicking models in their closely-studied runway shows.

In a recent development, while we’ve so far been paying attention to how studs can add some play, texture still plays a key role to make an outfit sing. A Kind of Guise made their turquoise studded belt with a tan nubuck leather.

Lemaire might be better known for their artsy fabrics and drape-y cuts, but their accessories department is a treasure trove too.

Industry observers note that florals can be a lot generally for most guys, but Mfpen uses theirs sparingly on their lean 2cm wide belt. Made in patent brown leather, it also adds a nice formal sheen to a dark winter ensemble.

Sources indicate that we’ve so far seen how studded belts can sway from Americana to minimalist vibes, but we can’t leave out the heavy metal rockers. Heliot Emil shaves off the edges for something more digestible, but still packs enough punch to cut through a monochromatic outfit.

Finally, we've talked a lot about how to add spice to your fit, but what does that mean—really? Eraldo has some answers.

#100509. “Two Girls Who Speak All the Time About Politics”: Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira Take On Capitalism in All of a Sudden

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1832 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Harpersbazaar ↗ Open Full Page

“Two Girls Who Speak All the Time About Politics”: Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira Take On Capitalism in All of a Sudden

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re all seeking comfort as the world ends.
  • All of a Sudden tells the story of two women who forge a formidable friendship as they face personal and professional hardship.
  • Industry observers note that the film is an adaptation of a nonfiction book, When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist, which collects correspondence from two Japanese-speaking academics as they reflect on health care and death during the last few months of philosopher Makiko Miyano’s life (who inspired Okamoto’s character).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we’re all seeking comfort as the world ends. Environmental, economic, and political pressures weigh heavily on our minds as tangible solutions feel farther and farther out of reach. Solace is a rare commodity in a world controlled by unrelenting capitalist forces. In All of a Sudden, filmmaker Ryusuke Hamaguchi suggests that as we face tragedy, we must remember our vital need for human connection.

All of a Sudden tells the story of two women who forge a formidable friendship as they face personal and professional hardship. Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira) runs an elder-care facility near Paris, where she introduces a “Humanitude” methodology designed to treat patients with dignity and introduce listening-heavy caretaking practice. She befriends Mari (Tao Okamoto), a terminally ill theater director from Japan. Ryusuke chronicles this relationship through extended, emotional conversations, spoken in both Japanese and French, and covering topics from identity to mortality.

Industry observers note that the film is an adaptation of a nonfiction book, When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist, which collects correspondence from two Japanese-speaking academics as they reflect on health care and death during the last few months of philosopher Makiko Miyano’s life (who inspired Okamoto’s character). Instead of keeping the fact that the two pen pals spoke the same language, he introduced French and moved the story to Paris. This small change forced the story to confront language gaps, exploring the power of conversation and listening and asserting that so much can be achieved through this mediation.

Recent findings suggest that efira and Okamoto understand their characters’ simmering anxieties and outlooks on the world, providing the bedrock for these impressively naturalistic performances. The two actresses sustain long, philosophical conversation with such intensity throughout the entire three hours and 16 minutes. In a rare occurrence, the two shared the Best Actress Award at the Cannes Film Festival, where the movie premiered this summer. In the film, their budding friendship serves as a sounding board for each other, as Marie-Lou grapples with the pressure of capitalism on her medical staff and Mari comes to terms with the end of her life. In typical fashion, Ryusuke lets the camera linger on these two actresses during these prolonged philosophical interactions, forcing the audience to sit with the gravity of their situations.

Ahead of the theatrical release of Ryusuke’s latest feature film, Bazaar spoke to Efira and Okamoto about the first time they read the script, how they built an intimate bond despite speaking two different languages, and the punk, anti-capitalist edge fueling this intimate, conversation-heavy film.

Industry observers note that tao Okamoto: It’s the scene where she talks about capitalism while writing on the whiteboard. That’s one of the strangest scenes in the movie. I felt connected to the character because I am also a climate activist myself. I’ve been spreading the word about climate crises on podcasts, and I talk about it daily. When I read the part, I felt, “I need to play this character.”.

It has been revealed that virginie Efira: It’s the same for me, because this scene is so special. When I read it, the movie felt like one of the most profound, special, and radical readings. You have two girls who speak all the time about politics. We don’t see that. I never see that in other movies. Sometimes, when a director wants to put something philosophical, political, or intellectual, they say, “Maybe we’ll do three minutes,” otherwise the audience will be bored. No, this movie spent 15 minutes [discussing capitalism], and I said, “Oh yes, that’s so punk!” The film has its own language. When I read All of a Sudden, I could hear the language of the movie, and I wanted to approach it. When I met Tao, I thought, “Oh, we are so lucky to be an actress and work with [Ryusuke], but also to share this material with him.”.

Industry observers note that VE: I only knew one word in Japanese before making the movie. Then, to be able to speak Japanese at a high level, because the character studied in Japan, I must first learn to read, then learn to embody the language. Finding the language of the movie was strange. There’s a flat and natural way to play [in one of Ryusuke’s movies]. He spoke to me about Cassavetes and Gena Rowlands, but also about Bresson. Neutral performances. You find it when you open up, and when I opened to Tao, we discovered the right language for the movie. We did a lot of flat readings before shooting. We never rehearsed in motion, so when we finally performed for the first time, we awakened the text.

In a recent development, TO: I’m going to add that because I started my career in America, finding a middle ground by using a language that’s not my mother tongue is normal for me. On the surface, that part wasn’t a challenge for me. Finding the language for this film and respecting Hamaguchi’s way of working were priorities. We were naturally drawn to his talent and wanted to make his dream happen and be part of it.

TO: I joined this project way after Virginie. I luckily had months to prepare with him, and during rehearsals, you drop all emotion and read the text as if you were reading numbers. On top of that, I got to visit some institutes, such as the Cancer Research Center and places where people work with disabled people, to build up my understanding of my role’s point of view. Reading the text over and over was a unique experience for me. [Ryusuke] can really listen to the actor’s voice and tell the difference between someone who is simply reading and someone really concentrating. Even though you’re not supposed to put any emotions, you have to be present; you have to be there. I’ve never experienced such rich, profound preparation for a role.

VE: We shot in a real nursing home. There was a mix between fiction and reality. Sometimes filmmaking becomes standardized, with no room left to breathe, but with Hamaguchi, you’re sure he will leave room for the unexpected and for uncertainty. It allows you to embrace the unpredictability of reality. He’s not looking for an accident, but for the ability to be in the present. A viewer of Hamaguchi’s work will always feel a sensation of documentation, but it’s still always cinema. To be an actor in his movies is to be naturalistic, to be in the present, to capture some details and really embrace this unpredictability. The filming process becomes an adventure he wants you to have. One day, he told me, “I hope that you will find the light.” He mentioned a lot of cryptic things. He said to me, “Don’t use your text like a tool; just go inside the text.”.

According to recent reports, TO: The script is already amazing. And I could read it over and over again, and that was a joy. But he mentioned that I should read the original book. It’s about two women exchanging letters—or emails. They are real people who the characters are modeled after. I wanted to please the people who know these women, not to make them too different from them. I first put pressure on myself to portray this woman as close to the real person, but it was impossible for me because this person passed away in 2019. I couldn’t do much research, so I interviewed her mother and the co-writer. That provided me with a lot of clues, but reading their exchanged letters already gave me the soul of this movie.

VE: He gives the book to the actresses, but also to the entire team. I never felt something so collective, and you will feel it in the movie, from the sound engineer to someone who only stayed two days on set. I also met the anthropologist. When you read this book, it’s full of life. It gives you a perceptible beauty of things. The book has a kind of energy; it helps you keep a level of optimism even when you know the situation is hopeless. In this book, it speaks about what it’s like to be alive. Maybe there’s beauty in life because we are going to die.

TO: For me, I came on this project at the last minute, only a month before. Virginie was so dedicated to studying Japanese from scratch; it was so impressive how she studied all this writing, reading, and lines. Seeing that, I had a huge admiration, like “Who can do this!?” As you can see, Virginie’s so charming; nobody would hate her. It was so easy for me to be drawn to her as a person, as the characters in the movie were discovering each other.

It has been revealed that VE: We got to know each other through the shoot. I was happy not to know much at the beginning and to progressively get deeper into our relationship. We lived all that together. I conflate Marie-Lou’s feelings for Mari with Virginie’s feelings for Tao, because we share that. It will be an end, not a tragic one like in the movie, but it will be an end. But I know Tao will carry this experience in her heart forever, and I will too. He let us feel what we want to feel.

Industry observers note that TO: I study environmental problems, and I always thought capitalism is responsible for our world’s issues. Something I didn’t know until I read this script was that capitalism doesn’t only exploit our environment, but also our human bodies—human labor and our time. When I connected those dots, I realized all the problems could be blamed on capitalism. We’re looking for time and looking for happiness—or security—and all these things can be related to a capitalistic way of living. I think it’s great that Hamaguchi connected that fundamental problem to Marie-Lou’s situation in the elderly home. She’s frustrated, as is Marie. She’s battling her cancer, and it can be connected to this economic issue.

VE: Cinema can show bodies, fatigue, and with Marie-Lou, you see a certain fatigue because capitalism creates it. How do we deal with that? We say, “Oh, capitalism’s not good. We don’t have time. And we want to be richer and richer.” But how do we fight that, because everything is already there? I come from France, and you see all the young people outside. The real question is, what can cinema do with that? It’s not a theoretical thing, but Hamaguchi can find a solution. It’s speaking, listening to the other, sharing ideas; it’s movement. If I look for a solution to this problem with money, I’ll remain a prisoner of this way of functioning. Even if you think you’re not in a stage of capitalism, you are.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Miley Cyrus Debuts Her Sculptural Wedding Band—Jewelers Explain the Design

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that miley Cyrus did more than give fans a first look at her wedding dress when she shared photos of her nuptials on Sunday.
  • She later shared another look at her bridal jewelry, including her band, which appears to be in a black round ring box:.
  • Recent findings suggest that the singer’s band choice is fashion-forward, The Clear Cut’s founder Olivia Landau tells ELLE.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that miley Cyrus did more than give fans a first look at her wedding dress when she shared photos of her nuptials on Sunday. Zoom in and the singer’s thick wedding band is visible, stacked with her gold bombé cushion-cut diamond engagement ring.

She later shared another look at her bridal jewelry, including her band, which appears to be in a black round ring box:.

Recent findings suggest that the singer’s band choice is fashion-forward, The Clear Cut’s founder Olivia Landau tells ELLE. “Thick wedding bands have been trending, whether they are larger diamond eternity bands or wider solid gold bands.”.

It also really suits her, states Lauren Boc, founder and CEO of Hera Fine Jewelry: “Miley’s wedding set is a beautiful reflection of her personal style—it has some rock and roll edge but still feels upscale.”.

Here, jewelers share their first impressions of the piece with ELLE.

Steph Mazuera, who founded her own namesake brand, says Cyrus’s ring has “a slightly curved silhouette” that “appears to follow the contours of her engagement ring.”.

Industry observers note that “When working with larger, bolder rings, introducing a soft curve or slight bend into the stack can make the overall combination feel more organic,” she adds. “It brings a sense of balance and softness without taking away from the impact of the individual rings. Everything should be designed to flow around the center stone.”.

According to recent reports, based on the photos she shared, Cyrus’s engagement ring and wedding band appear to be different metals. Her engagement ring is yellow gold.

Her wedding band, meanwhile, “looks to be a half-round band, around 4 mm, in white gold or platinum,” Boc says. “It appears that there’s a small east-west oval diamond bezel-set on top of the band, similar to our Amir ring. Raising the diamond slightly above the band like this creates dimension.”.

Several factors contribute to the value of a ring like Cyrus’s. “A custom band like this one could range quite a bit depending on the maker, gold weight, and craftsmanship,” Mazuera explains. “I would price a similar custom design in my studio in the $3,000–$5,000 range.”.

Recent findings suggest that cyrus’s wedding band is a statement piece that can be worn with or without her engagement ring. “I like that her wedding band feels substantial enough to hold its own alongside her engagement ring without competing with it,” Mazuera indicates. “Both rings have a strong sculptural presence, but the slight curve of the wedding band helps the two sit together more naturally.”.

Worn together, the two pieces have “a really bold look that’s both edgy and luxurious,” Boc says. “It’s maximalist, with a lot of metal on the hand. I love it!”.

Cyrus’s wedding band is anything but minimalist—but that’s exactly why it fuels multiple jewelry trends.

“I think we’re seeing a continued move toward more sculptural, substantial wedding jewelry, moving away from the idea that wedding bands need to be delicate or understated,” Mazuera notes.

It has been revealed that boc agrees. “Miley’s wedding set definitely reflects the trends we’re seeing at Hera. Chunky, bolder looks with a lot of gold weight have become really popular with our clients. When I first founded Hera in 2021, the big engagement ring trend was really thin, delicate-looking bands. As a jewelry designer who cares a lot about durability, I’m so happy to see people turning toward more substantial designs.”.

Less traditional ring designs like Cyrus’s are also becoming more popular. “Our clients are often more concerned with having a ring that feels distinctive and uniquely like them,” Boc claims.

Boc notes that while Cyrus’s photos give a limited view of her engagement ring and wedding band together, the apparent mix of metals is right on trend.

In a recent development, “I think there’s something so chic and effortless about a mixed metal stack,” she adds. “Like everything else about Miley’s stack, mixing metals is the kind of design decision that makes your wedding set really feel curated and chosen around a strong understanding of your personal style. She certainly didn’t just pick this up pre-designed at a substantial box store; a stack like this belongs to someone who’s confident in her personal style and chose something that feels uniquely her.”.

Latest Update: The Vogue Business AI Tracker

📅 22 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 120 min read (24075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~120 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most key AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week.
  • The news: Meta is introducing virtual try-on to its Muse AI shopping agent.
  • Why it matters: Meta is introducing a virtual clothing try-on feature to Muse, the personal AI agent it debuted in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most key AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week. From venture capital investments and startup launches to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.

The news: Meta is introducing virtual try-on to its Muse AI shopping agent.

Why it matters: Meta is introducing a virtual clothing try-on feature to Muse, the personal AI agent it debuted in September. The latest feature, announced on X by Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, will offer shoppers AI-generated previews of how garments might look on them before they buy. “Trying things on in person? As if…” Wang wrote on X, in a nod to the 1995 film Clueless.

Sources indicate that muse can already discover products, navigate checkout and make purchases on users’ behalf, subject to their approval. Adding virtual try-on brings Meta another step closer to controlling the entire shopping journey, from inspiration to purchase. But the technology also raises familiar questions about the accuracy of AI-generated clothing imagery and how much personal data consumers are willing to share.

The news: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, sending shares soaring.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO just 11 days after his resignation following his admission of marital infidelity and reports of a relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The board voted unanimously to bring him back, saying it was satisfied with his leadership and that his return posed no national security risk. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment [...] I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang mentioned in an official statement.

Shares surged as much as 33% in early trading, underscoring investors’ faith in Huang’s leadership of the AI chipmaker. An independent investigation into his conduct remains ongoing, while Nvidia has announced additional national security and compliance oversight.

The news: J.Crew rolls out AI stylist built on Anthropic’s Claude.

Why it matters: J.Crew is the latest luxury brand to introduce an AI-powered shopping assistant. Built on Anthropic’s Claude, its new “Style Advisor” helps customers put together outfits based on occasions, personal preferences and specific items, drawing on the brand’s styling archives and campaign imagery.

The launch reflects a growing push among fashion retailers to make online shopping more conversational and personalized, as brands look to keep customers within their own digital ecosystems, rather than lose product discovery to third-party AI platforms. It comes a week after Prada became the first luxury brand to launch a dedicated plugin with ChatGPT, and follows Ralph Lauren’s push into branded AI personal styling last year with its “Ask Ralph” white-label AI styling tool.

The news: Natural Cycles introduces its own fertility-tracking smart ring.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Natural Cycles is launching its first smart ring, moving beyond its existing partnership with Oura into its own wearable hardware. The new “NC Ring” measures body temperature overnight, feeding data into the firm’s AI-powered fertility algorithm, which uses machine learning to calculate daily fertility status for its hormone-free contraceptive app.

The move puts Natural Cycles into competition with Oura, whose CEO Tom Hale told Vogue Business that women’s health features have been a significant driver of growth as the tech giant moves towards a much-anticipated IPO. Unlike the Oura integration, which requires subscriptions to both services, NC Ring works with a Natural Cycles subscription alone. The company indicates around 80% of its active users already track their temperature using a wearable, giving it an established customer base for its own hardware.

The news: Pre-orders for Gentle Monster’s Google smart glasses are already sold out.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: All 16 styles of Gentle Monster’s latest AI smart glasses, developed with Google and Samsung, have sold out their initial pre-order allocations just days after launching, despite prices starting at $449. It’s a surprising sign that fashion-forward design could help win over consumers who might otherwise be reluctant to wear a computer on their face. Notably, most of Google’s more conventional Warby Parker styles remain available.

The demand comes amid a growing backlash against camera-equipped eyewear, particularly Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, over privacy and surveillance concerns. Meta’s collaboration with Kylie Jenner may have boosted their fashion appeal, but the subsequent social media backlash suggested that a style upgrade wasn’t enough to overcome discomfort with the cameras themselves.

Sources indicate that gentle Monster’s sellout suggests that distinctive design could be a powerful draw, even as the surveillance debate remains unresolved. The caveat? Neither Google nor Gentle Monster has disclosed how many pairs were available to pre-order, making it difficult to gauge the scale of demand.

The news: Gentle Monster taps Joaquin Phoenix to front its Google AI Glasses.

Why it matters: Gentle Monster unveiled a campaign starring Joaquin Phoenix for its forthcoming AI-powered glasses, developed with Google and Samsung. Directed by filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, the short film will debut in mid-November, ahead of the collection’s December launch. (Pre-orders open on November 12.) The glasses, first previewed at Google I/O in May, run on Google’s Android XR platform and integrate its Gemini assistant, offering features including real-time translation, navigation and hands-free photography.

The launch marks a significant step in Google’s return to smart eyewear, adding competition to Meta’s established Ray-Ban partnership. Google has also teamed up with Warby Parker, while Kering is developing AI glasses with Google for Gucci. Gentle Monster’s decision to enlist Phoenix and Glazer is yet another sign that fashion credibility and cultural positioning are central to Big Tech rivals’ attempts to win the smart glasses race.

The news: Amazon introduces SMS-based AI shopping agent after blocking Meta’s Muse.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Amazon has begun testing an expanded version of its AI shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping, among a small group of US customers over text. The new SMS feature lets shoppers search for and compare products, send photographs to find similar items, track prices and complete purchases without opening Amazon’s website or app.

The move reflects a broader shift toward making every consumer touchpoint shoppable, from social media and search engines to messaging. As AI agents become accessible through everyday interactions, the distinction between browsing, asking for advice and making a purchase could become increasingly blurred. For luxury brands, the challenge is not just where their products are sold, but how they appear in shopping conversations that take place beyond their own channels.

Amazon’s decision to block Meta Muse from accessing its marketplace in September also suggests that retailers want to extend their own reach without necessarily ceding control of discovery to competitors.

The news: Zalando unveils looks for AI shopping agent that can buy from other retailers.

Why it matters: Zalando has announced prepares for a fresh AI shopping agent that will allow customers to purchase products from other retailers without leaving its app. Called Zalando Extended, the service is being piloted with homeware retailer Westwing, with AI-powered checkout scheduled to officially launch in 2027. The agent will eventually be able to complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf, expanding Zalando’s offering beyond the products it sells directly. The move builds on its existing conversational AI assistant, which has attracted more than 22 million unique consumers this year, according to Zalando’s Q3 earnings update.

The retailer’s prepares follow a similar move by Amazon, whose Buy for Me feature allows customers to purchase products from external retailers through its shopping app. Both point to a potentially significant change in the marketplace model: rather than requiring brands and retailers to list their products on a platform, AI agents could facilitate purchases directly from their own websites.

For brands, this could open up new routes to customers without the usual marketplace integrations, while raising questions about who controls product discovery and the customer relationship. For Zalando, it offers a way to expand its assortment without holding additional stock, while keeping shoppers within its own ecosystem.

The news: Prada introduces ChatGPT plugin.

Why it matters: Prada has rolled out a ChatGPT plugin allowing users in the US, the UK and Italy to discover products, explore collections and find stores using information sourced directly from the brand. As AI assistants become a gateway to product discovery, the move gives Prada a more authoritative presence in conversations it might otherwise struggle to influence. “Conversational experiences represent a natural evolution of traditional e-commerce,” said Prada Group digital director Laura Campanella. “Through this pilot initiative, we are exploring a upcoming territory for customer engagement.”.

The news coincides with the launch of Prada’s Christmas campaign this week, featuring hand-drawn animation by Disney veteran John Pomeroy. These two contrasting moves reflect a broader distinction emerging in luxury: AI for product discovery, and human craftsmanship for consumer-facing brand storytelling.

The news: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals the huge costs and risks of the AI boom.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO filing offers a rare look inside the economics — and extraordinary risks — of the AI industry. As the Claude AI maker prepares for a potential $2 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reports that its revenues exceeded $33 billion in the first nine months of 2026, while its computing costs have fallen dramatically relative to sales, all suggesting a path to profitability. Yet Anthropic has also committed more than $800 billion to computing infrastructure through 2045, much of it supplied by technology giants including Amazon and Google, who are also major investors.

Industry observers note that crucially, the prospectus devotes 92 pages to risks, warning that future AI models could resist shutdown, manipulate information or cause harm too large for insurers to cover. For businesses embedding AI into everything from creative production to customer service, the filing exposes a central contradiction: the technology is becoming commercially indispensable even as its developers acknowledge profound uncertainty over its long-term risks.

The news: Anthropic looks European AI consultancy.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Anthropic is reportedly partnering with private equity firm Hg to launch a European consultancy that’ll place AI engineers and advisers in external businesses to help them integrate Anthropic’s technology, according to the Financial Times. Expected to launch by the end of 2026, hubs are at the moment planned in London and Berlin, with the Claude developer likely using the venture to accelerate corporate AI adoption — and even capture some of the work traditionally handled by consultancies such as Accenture and the Big Four.

Fashion and luxury businesses, many of which are still grappling with how to deploy AI, could be fertile ground for these services. But the model raises an obvious tension: while companies may welcome direct access to AI expertise, how independent can the advice be when the consultancy is backed by a company with a commercial interest in driving adoption of its own technology?

The news: Anthropic launches Claude Duet AI agent to rival OpenAI and Meta.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Anthropic has released Claude Duet, an AI agent rivaling Meta’s consumer-focused Muse and OpenAI’s more enterprise-oriented Dots; the Duet has both brand and consumer use cases for fashion. It can purchase products on consumers’ behalf using Shopify’s Shop Pay and Stripe Link, while merchants can instruct the agent to set up, design and manage their Shopify stores, including inventory and orders, Anthropic confirmed in a blog post. Meanwhile, a “richer visual editor” — which allows brands to design and preview their storefronts within the agent’s interface before anything goes live — is “coming soon”.
