#100505. I Prepared for This A.I. Chaos Moment for Over a Year. Here Is What I’ve Learned.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2202 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

I Prepared for This A.I. Chaos Moment for Over a Year. Here Is What I’ve Learned.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something big was unfolding.
  • I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something big was unfolding. As air traffic halted, Microsoft 365 went down, and Chase Bank and dozens of important websites, including the NSA’s internal classified network, experienced an array of outages, it started to seem plausible that stuff the artificial intelligence whistleblowers have been warning us about (swarms of rogue agents, AI-powered cyber attacks) was happening already. How worried should we be about the AI apocalypse? On the one hand, Claude doesn’t even have hands, LOL. On the other hand, in a battle between AI and the creaky digital infrastructure that underlays all aspects of modern life, it wouldn’t require a superintelligence to launch the final spinning wheel of death.

I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories. During Covid, I stocked up on toilet paper and some bags of beans and rice (still unopened on my shelves) and shattered my collarbone mountain biking when we were all supposed to be hunkered down indoors during lockdown. But I also listen to a lot of podcasts. Enough that my friends and partner have told me that a digital detox might improve my mental health and, by extension, theirs. And, lately, the podcasts have sent me plunging into a Mach tuck of terminal anxiety.

Recent findings suggest that the Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky. “Should I be, like, stocking up my bunker now?” Kevin Roose, cohost of Machine Gods asked his guest Ben Buchanan, the first White House Special Advisor for AI. There’s an obligatory chuckle that talking heads do now when discussing the AI apocalypse in front of an audience. “A month ago we were talking about normal things, ha ha,” Steve Eisman, finance guru of The Big Short fame, mentioned on his podcast on October 12, “And now we’re talking about the end of the world.” But it’s hard to casually segue from the end of the world to Anthropic’s IPO and not sound like a crank. So that laugh leaks out, and maybe it’s just a joke?

According to recent reports, but count me as a genuine worrier. This week I withdrew enough cash in hundreds from a Bank of America branch that the teller started to interview me. “Doing some home renovations? Making a massive purchase?” he asked.

“No, I’m worried as shit about AI, and in case you haven’t noticed it, banks aren’t doing so well right now,” I replied. In line with me were several people who couldn’t pay their credit card bills online because the payment portal had gone down.

We’ve been hearing about the existential risk of AI for a while now. I got into it last year by reading Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares’s book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, after hearing Yudkowsky interviewed on Ezra Klein’s podcast. This is a terrible book for someone who’s prone to worry because it relies on nontechnical metaphors and colorful analogies. Superintelligence is like a chessmaster. You don’t need to know the moves it’ll make to be certain it wins. True! Superintelligence, they say, will be like a fresh species that is so much smarter than us that, if it doesn’t really really truly love us more than our own mothers and want to keep us alive, it will kill us all. The same way we crush ants when we build skyscrapers. There’s no malice toward us. We just got in the way.

Recent findings suggest that over the past year I—casually, at first—started amassing supplies. My adventure hobbies give me an excuse. I need this 6,500-watt generator for elk-hunting camp. These 400-watt EcoFlow solar panels power a giant battery so I can bring my Starlink Mini on camping trips. I listen to history podcasts, and these offer more inspiration. There was a recent NPR one about the Carrington solar flare of 1859, which fried telegraph wires across the country. An event like that, in 2026, might knock out the grid for months. Another good reason to be prepared. I tell my partner that it’s normal for us to keep 500 pounds of dry goods in the cupboards at all times. Everyone does this. We already have three 3,000-gallon cisterns. We live in the desert; they came with the house. Did we need another 400-gallon one? It was just laying in the neighbors’ yard. Why wouldn’t I hook that up to the gutters?

In a recent development, I spent a lot of the summer using AI to program an app for backcountry adventurers, so I knew firsthand it was already smarter than me. The doomsday chatter started to meet me where I was around the time of the Hugging Face incident in July. Then Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic in September so he could tweet that Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” On November 5, independent evaluator METR found that Anthropic’s AI was already helping build its own successors—roughly doubling the organization’s pace of progress and shifting expert predictions for major disruptions closer to the present. At the Hinton Lectures, in Toronto, OpenAI board member Paul Christiano calmly told the audience, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”.

Sources indicate that friends who are less prone to apocalyptic thinking than I am tend to point out that the people ringing the alarm about AI never spell out exactly which chess moves AI uses to kill us. But the week after the lecture, there was Christiano on another one of my podcasts, Dwarkesh Patel’s show, explaining one such scenario.

Industry observers note that first, rogue AI agents create mischief of one kind or another. Then, the Trump administration tells Americans that the only way to wrest power back from the bots is to have the military take control of all data centers, the AI companies, and shut down the internet. This feels like an authoritarian power grab. It sets up civil unrest against the backdrop of a heavily lopsided information war, in which it’s almost impossible to tell which side anyone is on. Have the bots compromised the humans? Are the humans using the bots? Judging by how well everyone agreed on the facts around things like Covid and the 2020 election, our expectations should be low for how we’d perform as a society. Which brings us to the question of guns.

I don’t think of myself as really owning any guns at all. I believe that the fastest way to get shot is to start getting into gunfights. I personally know exactly zero civilians who have solved a problem with a firearm, but I know many who have made problems, including my own mother.

About 15 years ago, she called me one day from the dog park sounding flustered. She liked to shop for musical instruments and power tools at ShopGoodwill.com, and lately the boxes had gone missing from her porch in Spokane, Washington. “You’re not going to set a trap, are you?” I asked. Our minds worked the same way.

According to recent reports, “Well, I already did,” she mentioned. And that was why she was hiding from the police in the dog park.

She’d left a decoy package on the porch. A woman came to grab it, and my mother burst through the door two-handing her Sig Sauer the way she’d been trained at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Georgia, when she was starting her encore career as a CBP officer after 9/11. The woman claimed to be returning the package, not stealing it. A standoff ensued. My mom eventually backed down and the lady called the cops. My mom never responded to the phone calls from the police, and the whole thing just went away.

Industry observers note that so when it comes to guns, I think, what am I actually going to use this for? To fend off hungry neighbors? To join a well-regulated militia and maybe become a dystopian warlord? Maybe it’s as simple as guns are addictive and it’s fun to ring the steel at 500 yards. I’ve put together a couple of rifles out of parts—an MDT chassis here, a Howa barreled action there—for other members of the family to hunt with, but I only do archery. And shotguns don’t really count as guns, especially when they’re the fancy break-action models with florid engravings of bygone scenes afield. “How many guns are in this house?” my partner wants to know. She really wanted to pin me down. “Counting the unmounted lower receiver stashed in the floorboards in the attic? Eight.”.

My name is Grayson, and I have somehow become a prepper. It has not made me better off. It has made me poorer, and it has put me into contact with seedier elements of the general populace. I have what psychologists call a bias toward action, when the best thing to do is probably nothing at all. And I listen to too many podcasts.

One of them, from a year ago, really stuck with me. It was an episode of the financial podcast Prof G Markets. On it, I heard Aswath Damodaran, the NYU Stern valuation professor, tell the show’s wunderkind British cohost, Ed Elson, what he was doing with his money. “There’s no place to hide in stocks,” Damodaran mentioned. “For the first time ever, I am looking at parking my money into one, cash, and two, collectibles or physical assets.” That a guy as sober as Damodaran was talking up baseball cards and physical gold coins was shocking.

It was less shocking when, this week, Barstool Sports personality Daniel “Significant Cat” Katz posted screenshots purporting to show internal discussions with Dave Portnoy and Jersey Jerry about warning staff to “buy all the gold and silver u can.” I have a quick word of warning for anyone considering following Jersey Jerry’s advice.

It has been revealed that back in October, I asked Claude (I know, it’s ironic) for a recommendation on a reputable place to buy gold coins. It gave me a Texas-based website that had the same look as all of the substantial financial institutions. I clicked around, added a handful of coins to a shopping cart, and clicked purchase, expecting to find a checkout on the next screen where I could do the math and input payment details.

According to recent reports, instead, the site showed me a congratulatory message, and an email soon arrived with strange looking numbers in it. It was explained to me that these were the routing numbers where I needed to wire a large five-figure sum. To my eye, it seemed shady. No thank you, I stated. Customer service was either a stern woman with an eastern European accent or a guy with a Jersey accent. Their position was that I had already committed to buy the gold, and they’d send debt collectors after me if I didn’t pay up. But they could cancel the order for only a few thousand dollars. More than a month later, I’m still disputing it and have involved the attorney general’s office in three states.

Men—and it is indeed mostly men—have been wrongly predicting the end of the world for centuries, from Nostradamus and the Millerites through to the panic over Y2K. What is it that makes us want to prepare? Somewhere in the deepest parts of my monkey brain, prepping hits in the same nerve as when we’d build forts as kids and want to see if they’d withstand a good storm. When a man builds a dam, he wants it to hold a flood. So whether the thing you’re prepping for is a substantial hurricane, a novel coronavirus, or rogue artificial intelligence, the threat is both a source of dread and wonder. For someone who otherwise suffers from depression, it’s extremely stimulating and a little delusional.

Sources indicate that after all, it’s a very narrow window of apocalypse that a prepper of my means can fantasize about. If the disruption is too small, I’ll be like the foolish Y2K dad with the basement full of Chef Boyardee. If the disruption is, indeed, the big one, then everyone, including the personal-plane-New Zealand-bunker-rocket-to-the-Moon money, is probably SOL. The rest of us will be left deciding whether to become the crazy gun lady or the person stealing packages off her porch to survive. In which case, why worry about rice and ammunition? I’d be better off living like some of the humans in The Dark Forest, the sequel to The Three-Body Problem. When the aliens finally arrived, they focused on throwing wild parties and having spontaneous orgies.

If the AI apocalypse hits my fantasy sweet spot—a few months of camping at home before humanity surveys our near-misses and reassembles with renewed clarity and purpose—I’ll be prepared. Maybe the worst comes to pass: economic collapse accompanied by novel bio weapons, loose nukes, and total loss of human agency. In that case, I’ll have the petty satisfaction of having been right. I can hit my group chat with the ultimate mic drop. Told ya.

You May Be Thawing Your Turkey Wrong—Here’s How To Avoid Spreading Salmonella

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint.
  • Industry observers note that frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option.
  • Making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint. And the most involved, time-consuming dish is undoubtedly the turkey. The centerpiece of your holiday table needs hours in the oven and at least a day of brining, but don't forget the time it takes to defrost beforehand, too.

Industry observers note that frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option. But they do require a little extra TLC and planning. So if you buy a frozen bird this year, you'll need to know how to work with it.

Making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely. Like chicken, turkey can spread Salmonella and other harmful bacteria. You should exercise caution at every stage of the process, including thawing, to avoid making your guests sick. Here’s what you should know.

The USDA states it's also safe to defrost turkey in cold water, but in our opinion, it's not worth the hassle. The best bet is to thaw it in the refrigerator, where the bird can gradually defrost at the safe temperature with less risk of bacterial growth. What you should never do: thaw it on the counter, in the garage, or with warm water.

These environments are less controlled and can expose the turkey to the temperature danger zone (between 40°F and 140°F), where germs grow rapidly. Even if the center of the turkey is still frozen, the thawed exterior can become a hotbed for Salmonella by the time you're ready to roast.

Recent findings suggest that roasted turkey drippings make great gravy. But raw turkey juice dripping all over your fridge? Not so much. Even shrink-wrapped birds can leak, so you should always store your turkey on a baking sheet or roasting pan while it thaws.

Food safety experts also recommend storing raw meat on the lowest shelf. That way, any leaks are less likely to drip onto other ingredients in your fridge.

We know you're probably keeping a lot of other ingredients in your fridge, so it can be hard to set aside extra room for the turkey. That said, it's a step worth doing. Giving your turkey plenty of personal space minimizes the risk of raw meat or its juices coming into contact with other ingredients.

According to recent reports, in the event that your turkey does contaminate another ingredient, here's what to know: Foods that won’t be cooked, like salad greens, should be tossed if they’ve come into contact with raw turkey juices. Cooking contaminated foods thoroughly can kill harmful bacteria, but you’ll also need to clean any surfaces the juices touched.

Turkeys are big, so they take a long time to thaw all the way through. The experts at Butterball say you should allocate a day for every four pounds of turkey if you're keeping it in the fridge. That means if you're working with a 16-pound bird, set aside four days just for defrosting. Once it's fully thawed, Butterball says your turkey will stay safe in the fridge for up to four days.

And on top of that, brining can make your turkey even more flavorful. If your frozen bird didn’t come pre-seasoned, consider setting aside another day or two for that step. (Want some guidance? Check out our brining guide.).

According to recent reports, it’s extremely notable to keep things clean while you’re handling a turkey. One of the most common ways Salmonella spreads in the kitchen is through cross-contamination caused by poor hygiene.

Recent findings suggest that so wash those hands (including under your fingernails!) with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Make sure you also thoroughly clean any utensils and surfaces that come into contact with raw turkey or its juices using hot, soapy water.

And above all, don’t stress! Americans prepare millions of turkeys every Thanksgiving, so you're not alone in your turkey-roasting journey. Follow the tips above to ensure yours turns out safe to eat and delicious.

#100501. Tech Report: How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

Tech Report: How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain health isn’t just an issue for the elderly.
  • It has been revealed that the good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp.
  • Sources indicate that the method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain health isn’t just an issue for the elderly. Maybe you've experienced the first subtle signs of decline. Sometimes it’s a name that’s on the tip of your tongue. Or perhaps you've read a news story in the morning that you can't remember by the evening. It could be that you're feeling increasingly mentally fatigued after a typical day spent dealing with emails, text messages, phone calls, and constant interruptions.

It has been revealed that the good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp. “Our brain needs to be stimulated, at any age," notes Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan, and president of Assomensana, an association founded in Monza, Italy in 2004 to promote cognitive health. Routines help conserve mental energy, while new experiences force it to work,” says Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan. While working with people suffering from neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s, he came up with the idea to create a gym for the brain. “I asked myself what could be done earlier, when people are still healthy,” he remarked. His studies led him to develop a protocol that anyone can integrate into their daily routine.

Sources indicate that the method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience. This ability persists throughout one’s entire life, although it changes with age. Today, Iannocari's courses consist of weekly 90-minute sessions in groups of up to fifteen participants. Each session features about ten exercises focused on memory, attention, language, reasoning, creativity, and other cognitive skills. At the beginning and end of the program, twelve mental functions are assessed to measure their progress. “In our tests, we observe an average improvement in the overall cognitive efficiency index of 25–30%," says Iannoccari. "Some functions, such as attention and language, respond particularly well. Others, such as logical reasoning and prose memory, require more intensive work.” These results are based on the association’s experience and should not be interpreted as a percentage reduction in the risk of dementia. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, updated in 2026, acknowledge the potential benefits of cognitive training, while emphasizing that evidence regarding the long-term prevention of cognitive decline remains limited.

When it comes to our ability to concentrate, Iannoccari points to one culprit at the center of our modern lives. “Sometimes we feel tired not because we’ve done too many things, but because we’ve switched what we were doing too many times," he indicates. “Constantly switching from one task to another is more tiring than focusing on the same activity for an extended period.” A stream of notifications, information to process, and the need to respond rapidly to various requests put our attention to the test above all else. “It’s the foundation of all cognitive processes. When it’s fragmented, even the quality of the information we’re able to acquire deteriorates.”.

The Johns Hopkins professor recommends some tips you may know—and a few that might surprise you—to keep your brain firing on all cylinders.

It has been revealed that and then there’s AI, which promises to free us from an ever-increasing number of tasks. What are the consequences for our brains? “If we ask artificial intelligence to compare two tables, perform an analysis, and write a report, we get the work done in a few minutes that would previously have taken an entire day," says Iannoccari. “Saving work also means reducing some mental activity. But it depends on how we use these tools.”.

For Iannoccari, the key is to preserve two abilities: critical thinking and analysis. “We must know how to formulate questions, and this requires familiarity with the subject,” he indicates. “Then we must evaluate the answers, recognize any inconsistencies, and verify the information. Only a well-trained mind can spot errors.” This concern also applies to seemingly beneficial habits, such as reading books or solving crossword puzzles.“ Reading is invaluable, especially for the emotions it evokes and the worlds it allows us to discover," he says. “But reading doesn’t automatically mean memorizing. If we want to remember what we’ve read, we must do so with the intention of being able to recount it to someone else.” As for puzzle-solving pastimes, “Sudoku trains certain concentration and planning skills, while crossword puzzles stimulate the retrieval of information from memory,” he says. “These are useful activities, but a structured program allows you to work on different skills and gradually increase the difficulty of the exercises.”.

In addition to guided sessions, Iannoccari suggests short daily sessions he calls “Brain Breaks”— five-minute breaks for small exercises that counteract brain aging. “If we wait to find five free minutes, we’ll probably never find them.” “We need to make it a habit, just like having a cup of coffee.” Here are five exercises you can try:.

Recent findings suggest that choose a topic—preferably a positive one—read it carefully, and try to recount it to three different people without constantly referring back to the text. “The first time we repeat a piece of information, we’re often uncertain,” says Iannoccari. “The second time, we become clearer and more fluent. The third time, we have another chance to reinforce it in our memory.” It’s an exercise that stimulates what’s known as “prose memory”—the ability to recall and process information we’ve read or heard. “Let’s imagine learning one piece of news a day for 365 days: how much knowledge will we have accumulated?”.

In a recent development, for five minutes, write down as many words as possible that start with the letter A, trying to be quick. Repeat the exercise the next day, avoiding words you’ve already used. On the third day, move on to B, and so on. “It’s a way to train verbal fluency and lexical retrieval, particularly useful when we start to experience that ‘word on the tip of my tongue’ phenomenon,” notes Iannoccari. The goal is to gradually make the search more challenging by striving to find words that aren’t immediately obvious.

Right-handed people can try performing some simple tasks with their left hand, and vice versa. Open a drawer, move small objects, draw, and gradually try writing. “This newly introduced challenge forces the brain to break out of its automatic routines and engage resources we normally use less," he says. “Surprising results can be achieved: people who initially can’t even draw a line gradually learn to write with their other hand.” Of course, it’s best to choose safe activities and proceed without rushing.

Industry observers note that how many phone numbers do we still remember? And how often do we rely on the GPS even to get to relatively familiar places? “Before calling someone, I try to remember their number," claims Iannoccari. “Before using a calculator, I do the math in my head. Before turning on the GPS, I try to figure out the route.” The same goes for the grocery list. “I write it down so I can be sure I won’t forget anything, but at the supermarket I first try to recall the items. Only then do I check the list.” These are small opportunities to keep practicing skills that we increasingly tend to delegate to digital tools.

It has been revealed that once in bed, instead of focusing on the next day’s commitments, try to mentally retrace the day that just passed. What time did you wake up? What did you eat? Who did you meet? What did you talk about? What details stood out to us? “You have to try to be very detailed,” states Iannoccari. “Often, people who have trouble falling asleep find that this exercise also helps them drift off.”.

It has been revealed that but there’s another aspect that’s particularly close to his heart. “I find there’s something romantic about it. We live one day after another and often retain almost nothing of them. Reflecting on it means recognizing its value. Every day leaves something behind, like a geological layer deposited on top of the one before it.” This little ritual offers an opportunity to recall the experiences we wish to preserve.

It has been revealed that when is the right time to start? “As children,” says Iannoccari. “We encourage them to play sports, but we rarely think about the importance of training mental abilities just as intentionally.” In adult life, of course, exercise, sleep, nutrition, stress management, and social relationships also matter. “But if I had to name three drivers of the mind, I’d choose curiosity, creativity, and emotions."he says. "Curiosity opens us up to new knowledge, creativity allows us to connect that knowledge in original ways, and emotions make experiences more memorable.”.

A conversation with neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett on the counterintuitive ways your mind processes reality—and why understanding that might help you feel a little less anxious.

In a recent development, he also notes that, though older age is associated with worse brain function, it's also how we collect the wisdom of lived experiences. “We think an efficient brain is the one we had at twenty, and we lose sight of what we’ve gained by the time we’re sixty or seventy," he indicates. "When we were young, we may have been faster, but over time we’ve accumulated skills, knowledge, and experience. We possess a much richer worldview.”.

It has been revealed that the real challenge is to remain present to ourselves and others, valuing who we’ve become.” And perhaps, as the years go by, one of the most important skills is precisely learning to choose where to invest our mental energy. “We meet people who, now that they’re retired, are busier than when they were working. We’ve come to associate efficiency with the number of things we can do, but in doing so, we lose the opportunity to delve deeper, reflect, and let experiences settle. I always say that I don’t pursue nice ideas—I pursue great ideas. Because there are so many nice ideas, and they risk scattering our energy in a thousand different directions.” “With age,” concludes Iannoccari, “we have a great privilege: the ability to choose.”.

#100499. The Year Fashion Fakes Became Too Real

The Year Fashion Fakes Became Too Real

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Celebrities can be seen wearing clothes they’ve never touched, luxury houses may appear to release products they’ve never designed, and, in some cases, even clothes that actually exist don’t quite look like themselves online.
  • In a recent development, earlier this month, the embattled Nvidia co-founder and now reinstated CEO Jensen Huang became an unlikely menswear sensation when the Instagram account @hidden.ny posted images of him wearing an archival, silver-studded Saint Laurent leather jacket from Hedi Slimane’s tenure.
  • Sources indicate that the internet rushed to crown Huang a Hedi boy, but he’d never worn the jacket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fashion has a reality problem. Celebrities can be seen wearing clothes they’ve never touched, luxury houses may appear to release products they’ve never designed, and, in some cases, even clothes that actually exist don’t quite look like themselves online.

In a recent development, earlier this month, the embattled Nvidia co-founder and now reinstated CEO Jensen Huang became an unlikely menswear sensation when the Instagram account @hidden.ny posted images of him wearing an archival, silver-studded Saint Laurent leather jacket from Hedi Slimane’s tenure. The post came just a day after Nvidia opened an investigation into Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy. “Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy,” read the caption.

Sources indicate that the internet rushed to crown Huang a Hedi boy, but he’d never worn the jacket. As CNN first revealed, the images were fake; Vanity Fair subsequently verified they’d been generated or altered using AI. The originals, in fact, showed Huang wearing Dior at an airport in Seoul in June. The post was subsequently taken down, but the fantasy had already traveled.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang waves to the media as he arrives at Gimpo airport in Seoul on June 5, 2026. Photo: Jung Yeon-je / AFP via Getty Images.

Days later, designers including Reese Cooper and Gerrit Jacob called out luxury retailer Ssense over product imagery that misrepresented their clothes, from distorted construction details to inaccurate branding. Unlike Huang’s fictional fashion moment, these were real garments available to buy.

Cooper, founder of Reese Cooper and RC Outdoor Supply, discovered the inaccuracies while browsing the website himself. He had not been consulted about the imagery, which depicted his brand’s signature trademarked hook at twice its actual size.

“There’s a lot of sewing and design detail inaccuracies but the important problem is misrepresenting my trademarks — our hook is a major part of our branding, and of course all of the logos,” Cooper indicates. “The initial reaction is disappointment and frustration. It takes an overwhelming amount of time and resources to protect your brand legally with these trademarks, not to mention the work going into designing the clothes themselves.”.

The errors were subtler than AI signifiers of the past, like extra fingers or missing limbs. But when shopping online, details matter. Fashion commentator and journalist Odunayo Ojo identified missing design details and Gerrit Jacob trousers with an invented waistband, additional seams and altered lettering.

“AI pulls everything toward an average, but design lives in the details that depart from that average,” Ojo states. “Generative models are built to make something that looks plausible, not something that’s precise. Plausible is fine for a moodboard. On a product page, plausible is misrepresentation.”.

In a statement to Vogue Business, a spokesperson for Ssense acknowledged the errors: “Accurate representation of our brand partners and their products is fundamental to Ssense. We recognize that some recent e-commerce imagery did not meet that standard, resulting in inaccuracies in product details. We take full accountability and have taken steps to resolve this issue with urgency.”.

It comes after local media reported over the summer that Ssense had laid off its full-time photography and retouching teams as it invested in AI Virtual Try-On (VTON) in August to support content production and has since strengthened quality controls. The spokesperson for Ssense confirmed to Vogue Business that “in preparation for the transition to Virtual Try-On (VTON), Ssense made organizational changes in June that affected certain roles within its visual content department.” Ssense did not explicitly confirm that the AI technology caused the inaccuracies last week.

Together, the incidents exposed two sides of fashion’s growing synthetic image problem: AI can make an imaginary garment look real, and a real garment look imaginary, with both able to put brands in a difficult spot.

The Huang images were far from an isolated incident. In April, AI-generated images showed celebrities including Megan Fox and Robert Pattinson wearing fictional Balenciaga designs made from cardboard shipping boxes, while another fake imagined the Olsen twins in a Louis Vuitton campaign.

Industry observers note that nor was Ssense the only case of AI imagery creating confusion around real products. In May, after Swatch and Audemars Piguet teased a collaboration, AI-generated images of a colorful Royal Oak wristwatch circulated online. The actual release was a collection of Bioceramic pocket watches, disappointing fans who had come to expect a product that never existed.

Sources indicate that while the average person has struggled to distinguish many AI-generated images from real photographs for a couple of years, experts say things seem worse now because it’s become so much easier to produce them. “It’s now at the point where it’s really easy to create highly realistic content with minimal knowledge of how to optimize for the tool you’re using, and there’s plenty of tools to choose from,” says Henry Ajder, a synthetic media expert and founder of Latent Space Advisory, pointing to their integration into popular chatbots and the growing availability of open-source alternatives.

Fashion is particularly exposed. “With fashion imagery, because there’s so much highly stylized, high-quality content associated with the industry, there’s been a huge amount of training data for these tools to utilize,” Ajder claims, arguing that we’ve reached a tipping point. In 2026, unofficial campaigns can now look practically indistinguishable from a house’s own advertising, even as brands experiment with AI themselves.

It has been revealed that for Cooper, the Ssense episode has created a commercial dilemma. “Simply put, it’s brand damage,” he indicates. “RC Outdoor Supply is a upcoming company and all we have is our trademarks and reputation of design aesthetic and quality. To have these things put in question by the customer, it really erodes trust for the brand as a whole.”.

He points out that retailers judge brands on sell-through, and inaccurate listings can deter purchases or generate returns, while removing them means losing sales altogether. “Ssense has removed the images, which I’m thankful for. However, it also removed the ability for anyone to purchase those items, which will result in low sales when looking at this season’s data,” Cooper notes.

Sources indicate that experts say the problem is particularly acute in luxury, where small design decisions and fit often underpin a garment’s value. “In luxury, the details are the price,” Ojo claims. “If the image erases them, you’ve erased the reason the garment costs what it costs — the problem isn’t AI as a tool, it’s using it for the one job where accuracy is the whole point.”.

Industry observers note that an accurate image of Reese Cooper’s Outdoor Supply Sierra Puffer Jacket. Photo: Screenshot, rcoutdoorsupply.com, courtesy of Reese Cooper.

Recent findings suggest that wholesale contracts, meanwhile, haven’t caught up. “When a retailer’s AI imagery misrepresents a garment, the designer absorbs the returns and the reputational harm, and most of the wholesale agreements I review do not address AI-generated product imagery,” states Shermin Lakha, founder and managing attorney at Lvlup Legal.

For luxury brands, the legal questions become more complicated when AI-generated images of their products circulate online without anything being sold, as in the Huang case. Lakha argues that luxury brands have fewer remedies against these non-commercial viral fakes than many might assume. “Existing law is effective against commercial actors and leaves a gap for the viral fake that nobody monetizes,” she states. Susan Scafidi, founder of the Fashion Law Institute at Fordham Law School, agrees legal options are limited. “There is no single, universal cause of action that a brand can invoke to target unauthorized imagery that includes its products, whether that imagery is created by AI or not,” she says. Trademark and false advertising claims may apply where recognizable products or logos are involved; other claims may arise from reputational harm.

The calculation changes if an account uses a brand’s identity to sell services, promote counterfeit goods or generate revenue. The Balenciaga cardboard box images, for example, were associated with an account promoting a course on creating viral AI visuals. But even when brands have grounds to challenge unauthorized imagery, the distinction between infringement and creative expression is rarely straightforward. “Luxury brands have for decades chafed against the imprecise nature of parody and other forms of ‘fair use’ under US law,” indicates Scafidi.

Industry observers note that daniel Shapiro, a brand protection executive at Red Points, which helps brands detect counterfeits and online impersonation, says traditional monitoring tools that look for logos are increasingly inadequate. Newer systems analyze entire images for unreleased colorways, inaccurate hardware or recognizable patterns, even when logos have been removed.

But policing the internet is only part of the answer. Scafidi urges brands to distinguish harmful images from passing memes to decide whether to take action. When necessary, brands can work with platforms on removals and respond through their own channels. Lakha also recommends tighter contracts and internal verification before brands share viral images.

Sources indicate that on brand and retailer sites, Ojo wants human review against physical garments, designer approval and disclosure of AI alterations. “If what’s on the page isn’t a photograph of the real garment, they [a designer] should say so,” he says. “A small [AI] label costs nothing. Finding out later is what causes scandals and also costs Ssense the customer,” he says.

The deeper challenge may be cultural. Luxury has traditionally relied on controlling its image, from campaign casting to the placement of a logo. AI makes that harder, while increasing the value of visual credibility. Lizzie Wheeler, founder of archival bridal salon Studio Dorothy and the resale expert behind the Instagram account @shit.u.should.buy, sees consumers becoming more discerning and brands returning to human craft as a ‘realness’ signal.

Sources indicate that “Aside from the legal issues, luxury is moving back toward more organic, human work (like the hand-drawn Prada holiday campaign) and showing AI shortcuts will dissuade a luxury client,” she says. “Ssense does rely heavily on the luxury client and I imagine this type of error will impact them seriously,” she adds.

Sources indicate that the irony is that fashion’s most elaborate fakes have often been powered by some of its most recognizable signatures: a Balenciaga provocation, an archival Saint Laurent jacket, an instantly identifiable luxury watch. As these signatures become easier to imitate, the ability to prove what’s real is becoming a more valuable part of luxury itself.

“The consumer is becoming increasingly educated,” Wheeler says. “So I’d advise all retailers against pulling wool over the customer’s eyes.”.

Fascia Release Is the Key to Regulating Your Nervous System, Getting Better Sleep, and Improving Skin

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’m curled up on a treatment bed in the Corinthia spa, feeling a knot of tension dissipate slowly from my neck and shoulders.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Fascia is deeply connected to the entire sensory network,” explains Nadia Alibhai, a London-based osteopath who was unfazed by my heightened emotions.
  • It has been revealed that once dismissed as mere biological wrapping paper, fascia—made up of water, collagen, elastin, and hyaluronic acid—is now understood as a living, three-dimensional web.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’m curled up on a treatment bed in the Corinthia spa, feeling a knot of tension dissipate slowly from my neck and shoulders. Within minutes, tears prick my eyes. I’m familiar with the sudden catharsis bodywork can bring, but this is different. Known as “myofascial release”—a targeted therapy that works with fascia, the continuous matrix of connective tissue that wraps every muscle, nerve, and organ—it aims to reduce tightness and release restricted tissue, restoring its natural glide.

Recent findings suggest that “Fascia is deeply connected to the entire sensory network,” explains Nadia Alibhai, a London-based osteopath who was unfazed by my heightened emotions. “When you move or hold stress, forces are transmitted through this interconnected system. It senses everything and dictates how the whole body responds. This treatment directly influences how we perceive and react to tension.”.

It has been revealed that once dismissed as mere biological wrapping paper, fascia—made up of water, collagen, elastin, and hyaluronic acid—is now understood as a living, three-dimensional web. “It’s part of a complex system involving movement, circulation, lymphatics, posture, and tissue health,” Alibhai explains. When it works well, it keeps everything moving and prevents systems from becoming sluggish, but when it becomes restricted, often from scrolling, sedentary habits, or chronic stress, the fluid between the layers can thicken. This affects physical mobility and emotional well-being, leading to problems ranging from pain and stiffness to a dysregulated nervous system.

Fascia and neurology are intrinsically linked, explains skin-health expert Annee de Mamiel. “Fascia changes according to how we move, breathe, and repeatedly load the body,” she notes. “Cortisol and adrenaline change our physiology; the nervous system alters breathing, muscular tone, and stress response. Over time, these repeated patterns affect the tissues.” It’s a catch-22: greater stress can tighten fascia, which in turn can send your body into fight-or-flight mode, prolonging the anxiety that caused the damage in the first place.

This mind-body connection is just one reason why fascia has piqued the wellness industry’s interest. Google searches for “fascia release” have soared in the past year, while facials targeting the system are becoming more popular. Robert Schleip, the director of the Fascia Research Group at Ulm University, attributes this to its holistic possibilities. “Fascia is now studied in relation to the autonomic nervous system, and therefore emotional regulation, as well as the immune system and aging,” he indicates. The latest findings show that supporting your fascia goes far beyond easing a tight neck; it's linked to reduced arterial stiffness and improved cardiovascular health.

In a recent development, fascia release has also entered the skin-health conversation. Tight fascia can be an overlooked culprit behind loss of luminosity, puffiness, and premature aging, says de Mamiel, because it’s heavily involved in fluid drainage and lymphatic pathways. “The diaphragm plays a role in pressure changes and fluid movement through the body, and the fascial system connects these areas,” she explains. “When I work on movement and tension through the neck, chest, and rib cage, I often see a change in how congested or puffy the face appears.” However, releasing fascia effectively doesn't require aggressive force. “If I use so much pressure that your body braces, I’ve produced the opposite response—it’s about creating conditions where the nervous system and tissue can both settle.”.

It has been revealed that facialist Nichola Joss achieves similarly impressive results with her signature Inner Facial, which fuses lymphatic drainage, fascia release, buccal massage, and sculpting techniques. “Fascia surrounds and supports our muscles; when restricted, it affects how freely muscles move,” Joss explains. This affects lymphatic flow and your skin’s natural glow. “By releasing muscular and fascial tension, you lift, tone, and sculpt contours while boosting circulation and softening fine lines.”.

Beyond professional treatments, supporting fascial health depends on consistent daily habits. First, fascia thrives on varied movement: try walking, twisting your body, reaching overhead, and squatting to support overall health. Unfortunately, there are no true quick fixes: Spending the day glued to an office chair and then going straight into an intense HIIT session can actually be counterproductive. Instead, interrupt patterns throughout the day: Stand during phone calls instead of sitting, swing your arms gently during screen breaks, and make sure you’re not holding your breath during stressful periods at work. Counteract hours spent hunched over a device with this simple doorway stretch: Place your forearms against the frame, step forward gently, and hold for 20 to 30 seconds while breathing deeply.

Schleip recommends aligning exercise with your circadian rhythm. “Incorporate dynamic, elastic, or bouncing movements in the morning, ideally outdoors, and slow stretches in the evening,” he suggests, adding that sustained yoga positions, such as a child’s pose held for at least 30 seconds, can be particularly helpful. “Regular stretching improves joint mobility and may benefit cardiovascular markers such as arterial stiffness,” he adds. Finally, make nutrition and hydration a priority: fascia is 70 percent water and needs hydration to glide freely.

As Alibhai reflects at the end of my session: “The goal isn’t to constantly release fascia; it’s to keep your body moving, adaptable, and well nourished.” I leave feeling lighter and more grounded—and I instinctively skip the Tube and walk home.

The True Story of Ian Charleson, the Trailblazing Actor Andrew Scott Plays in Elsinore

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Elsinore, quite possibly this year's most moving film, Andrew Scott gives a captivating, awards-worthy performance as the late, great Scottish actor Ian Charleson.
  • "I'd rather die of Hamlet than die of AIDS," Scott-as-Charleson states in Elsinore, which opened in select theaters last week.
  • I remarked to him, It will kill you, which it did," Charleson's friend Sean Mathias, an accomplished actor and director in his own right, told me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Elsinore, quite possibly this year's most moving film, Andrew Scott gives a captivating, awards-worthy performance as the late, great Scottish actor Ian Charleson. Though he never became a household name, Charleson's star shone brightly in the early 1980s when he appeared in two consecutive Best Picture winners: 1981's Chariots of Fire and 1982's Gandhi.

"I'd rather die of Hamlet than die of AIDS," Scott-as-Charleson states in Elsinore, which opened in select theaters last week. This defiant line sums up the incredible coup de grâce that Charleson pulled off at the end of his life. When he began his valedictory stage run as Shakespeare's Danish Prince in October 1989, the 40-year-old actor was dying of AIDS. His face was so swollen with septicemia that the cast, crew, and audience at London's National Theatre were told he was recovering from a sinus operation.

"I begged him not to do Hamlet. I remarked to him, It will kill you, which it did," Charleson's friend Sean Mathias, an accomplished actor and director in his own right, told me. "The amount of energy it takes to play that kind of classical role, both physically and spiritually, would tire the most ardent athlete. For a man dealing with the onslaught of AIDS, it was almost impossible.".

According to recent reports, but against the odds, Charleson turned in a monumental performance. In a review for The Sunday Times, theater critic John Peter described his Hamlet as "virile and forceful" and wrote that the actor "oozes intelligence from every pore." Charleson's performance was all the more remarkable because he was an eleventh hour replacement for Daniel Day-Lewis, who left the production early—quite literally, midway through a performance—because he was so haunted by Shakespeare’s gothic tragedy.

"People still remember Ian's performance as Hamlet," states Andrew Scott, whose performance in the film captures Charleson in the tumultuous final year of his life. Elsinore's screenwriter Stephen Beresford believes it's fitting that no footage of Charleson's defining performance exists. "An important thing to remember about Ian is his extraordinary contradictions," he says. "He wants to be seen and not seen, to be known and not known." Charleson, in fact, was so publicity-averse—perhaps partly because he was a closeted gay man—that he walked out of the Chariots of Fire press junket.

At the same time, he was simply an old-school British thespian who believed that the work should speak for itself. "Ian was incredibly passionate about this extraordinary part of Hamlet," Scott adds, citing the actor's devotion to his craft as a major incentive in his decision to join Elsinore. "But the chief thing [I love about him] is his courage and sense of humor.".

Recent findings suggest that in Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson share his AIDS prognosis with his Hamlet castmates. When he died on January 6th, 1990, just seven weeks after his final curtain call, it was also disclosed to the public at large. At the time, Charleson's close friend Ian McKellen told the British press: "It is rare for anyone in the public eye to say that they are HIV positive, let alone that they have AIDS. It is a tribute to Ian that he should ask for the cause of his death to be made public and it is the most marvelous offer of support that he could have given to other men and women all over the world suffering from the AIDS virus.".

Beresford, who wrote Elsinore's screenplay after extensive conversations with Charleson's friends, family, and contemporaries, told me that it was actually the actor's father, Jack, who made the decision to disclose his cause of death publicly. "The tabloids were already circling, so I think there must have been fear that it was going to come out anyway," suggests Beresford, who previously penned the 2014 film Pride, which told the true story of gay and lesbian activists who raised money for the families of English coal miners during their 1984 strike.

Sources indicate that still, even if it wasn't carried out at his own behest, Charleson's posthumous contribution to HIV/AIDS awareness was very significant at a time when the disease was highly stigmatized and virtually impossible to treat. It would be another five years before HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) made the disease manageable.

According to recent reports, in the U.K., the actor has also been immortalized with the annual Ian Charleson Awards, which since 1991 has recognized the best classical stage performances by actors under the age of 30. Past winners include David Oyelowo, Andrea Riseborough, Paapa Essiedu, Rebecca Hall, and Jack Lowden, while Benedict Cumberbatch, Cynthia Erivo, and Jessie Buckley have all received runner's-up prizes or commendations. "Ian's name is legendary within the [British] theater because of what he achieved in Hamlet, and the awards were set up to keep his memory alive," Beresford notes.

It has been revealed that in Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson wryly lamenting the fact that, though he starred in the Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire, "all anyone can ever remember is its theme music." In this stirring sports biopic, Charleson played Eric Liddell, a devout Christian who managed to win gold at the 1924 Olympic Games despite withdrawing from his best event, the 100-meter sprint, because the heats fell on a Sunday. Charleson also appeared in the following year's Best Picture winner, Gandhi, as an Anglican priest who supported the iconic title character's fight for Indian independence.

In a recent development, sadly, despite these back-to-back triumphs, Charleson never made it as a bona fide movie star. By 1986, he was reduced to appearing in Car Trouble, a crass British comedy about a man who falls in love with his new convertible. "He was very disappointed that film stardom didn't prolong itself," indicates Mathias, who believes that Charleson's sexuality denied him further opportunities in mainstream movies. "He wasn't out [publicly], but everyone in the business knew he was gay. And back then, gay actors just weren't given work in Hollywood.".

Consequently, and perhaps aptly given his predilection for the stage, Charleson found salvation in the theater. On June 25th, 1989, he appeared in a one-night only revival of Martin Sherman's seminal queer play Bent. This pointed production at London's Adelphi Theatre, which also starred McKellen, Ralph Fiennes and Richard E. Grant, was staged to raise money for The Stonewall Group, a newly formed nonprofit that went on to become the U.K.'s leading LGBTQ+ rights organization. Charleson portrayed Greta, a drag performer who changes into male-presenting clothes during the play.

In a recent development, by this point, Charleson's torso was covered in lesions caused by Kaposi's sarcoma, a rare form of cancer common in AIDS patients. Mathias, who was directing the fundraiser, had screens erected on stage so that Charleson could change costumes out of view. "Ian remarked to me, But the crew can still see my body from the wings! So I said I'd get more screens put up," Mathias remembers. "But then he thought about it, and went, You know what? Fuck it! I always feel that was the moment, really, that he decided he would come out [as having AIDS].".

Shortly after Bent, Charleson was asked by Hamlet's director, Richard Eyre, to step in for Daniel Day-Lewis. Dickie Beau, an actor and writer who paid tribute to Charleson with his one-man stage show Re-Member Me (and who appears in Elsinore as the drag activist Sister Belladonna), believes Bent is a "truly significant" part of his legacy. “Not only did it help to kickstart [the charity] Stonewall, but it said a lot about him that he was happy to play Greta, who isn't a leading part,” he says. "Ian McKellen once said to me that, as much as Charleson saw himself as a lead actor, he was also a tech giant man.".

It's another of the fascinating contradictions that seem to make up Ian Charleson. Mathias notes he was generally "quiet and private" and "very masculine," but also possessed a "wonderfully camp sense of humor." There's a poignant irony in his becoming the subject of a major motion picture, Beresford says, laughing: "Ian would have hated this publicity tour. I can guarantee that absolutely no part of him is watching us today!".

For Scott, who embodies Charleson so beautifully that he’s considered an awards season frontrunner, Elsinore's purpose is simple: “I hope our movie continues his legacy.”.

In a recent development, part of the silhouette’s enduring popularity is its versatility. This season, in particular, the bucket bag is enjoying renewed attention, with everything from cinched drawstring closures and sculptural top handles to unexpected hardware giving the classic a fresh look.

When shopping for a bucket bag, consider more than just the looks. Think about how and where you’ll carry yours: A spacious style can double as a work tote, while a mini version can add a touch of whimsy to evening looks. Fortunately, there’s no shortage of choices, whether you’re looking to invest in a luxury piece or discover something at a more accessible price point.

According to recent reports, while preferences are unique to each shopper, the best options combine quality craftsmanship with functional details, from comfortable straps to secure closures and interiors that accommodate everyday essentials. Ahead, we’ve rounded up bucket bags to shop now, from understated versions to modern interpretations of the timeless silhouette.

Few materials make a handbag feel as luxurious as suede, particularly in wintertime. In rich shades of chocolate brown, navy, and burgundy, the tactile surface exudes sophistication. Just remember that suede requires care, particularly when water is involved.

According to recent reports, for anyone who carries their entire life in their handbag, oversized bucket bags offer a stylish alternative to traditional work totes, with enough room for a laptop, water bottle, and whatever else the day demands. Supple leather designs have a relaxed, lived-in appeal, while sturdier versions offer a professionally glossy finish. Look for a wide strap, a secure closure, and an organized interior to make the most of the extra space and keep it gentle on your shoulders during the commute.

In a recent development, there’s something undeniably charming about a drawstring closure, which gives bucket bags their signature gathered appearance (and helps keep belongings secure). The cinched opening creates visually impactful folds that look particularly elegant in buttery leather, soft suede, or evening-ready satin.

If your wardrobe leans minimalist, a structured bucket bag may be the perfect match. Unlike softer iterations that collapse when set down, these styles maintain their architectural structure thanks to firmer leather and well-constructed bases; longer straps also allow for crossbody wear. Their shape makes them feel more like design objects than everyday accessories, especially when finished with distinctive hardware.

Good things really do come in small packages, and mini bucket bags are proof. These scaled-down versions trade generous storage space for playful proportions that are ideal for evenings out, weekend intends, or occasions when you only need the essentials. Choose a style with a detachable strap for added versatility, or carry it by hand for a more dressed-up effect.

It has been revealed that woven bags have moved beyond their beach-vacation beginnings. Intricately interlaced leather lends the bucket silhouette an artisanal quality, while tightly bound raffia in darker shades is appropriate for city dressing. Look for details like leather handles and tonal finishes that give these textured designs a more elevated, winter-ready look.

For a ladylike approach to the bucket bag, consider a top-handle silhouette. Short, sculptural handles give the otherwise casual shape a more refined appearance. Some feature rigid circular handles, while others have softly curved leather straps that sit comfortably in the crook of the arm.

Apple Juice Bread

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level.
  • I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal.
  • Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard.

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

In a recent development, set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

In a recent development, transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very promptly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

Latest Update: What The Altruists Gets Right About Tech Scammers Like Sam Bankman-Fried

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the math holding up Netflix’s The Altruists is simple.
  • Recent findings suggest that famously, no bankers were sent to prison in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis.
  • One of the threads in the journalism about the crimes, and on The Altruists, is that our power couple did not feel good in fancy spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the math holding up Netflix’s The Altruists is simple. Anthony Boyle plays currently imprisoned one-time cryptocurrency king Sam Bankman-Fried, and Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison, fellow momentary crypto royal and Bankman-Fried’s one-time romantic partner. Both actors cook so fearlessly that the show’s shortcomings recede into the background. What you’re left with is a tidy sum: two excellent performances that offer rich, vatic examinations of real-life figures. From these visions of Bankman-Fried and Ellison we get a glimpse into a crime and into a psychology.

Recent findings suggest that famously, no bankers were sent to prison in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. No suit from Countrywide Financial walked the yard in Lompoc. But Samuel Bankman-Fried did go to prison after being found guilty of wire fraud and conspiracy. For the Bloomberg set, his trial was covered as intensely as O.J. Simpson’s, and each day of it hit trip wires: polycules, blockchain, non-fiat currency, etc.

One of the threads in the journalism about the crimes, and on The Altruists, is that our power couple did not feel good in fancy spaces. But unlike the protagonists of so many other demonstrates and movies from the tech-disruptor-story boom of the past 15 years, neither Boyle’s SBF nor Garner’s Ellison lean into rage.

It has been revealed that on The Altruists, SBF and his inner circle frequent a Margaritaville in the Bahamas. They seem happy there, or at least at home. To be wildly rich, extremely young, and crushing vegan nachos at Jimmy Buffett’s theme restaurant is a choice made out of avoidance.

The show’s first episodes make clear the overlaps between Ellison and Bankman-Fried. They were true math minds surrounded by the glib Wharton crowd, goofs with board games. They were not-conventionally-attractive people in an industry where many people are quite hot, and where the primarily hot at least know which regression tool best fits what task.

The Altruists’s versions of SBF and Ellison found love in a hopeless place. Boyle interviews Garner for a position at Jane Street and they realize they have the exact same investment strategy—all in, all the time. If you didn’t know better, you’d be rooting for these two off-putting lovebirds to make a go of it.

Boyle’s performance mesmerizes. He seems to have control over his lashes, so completely articulated is his eye acting. His whole posture changes as he takes up different roles in the story: a curious loser, a gifted rhetorician, an anxious boss, an ignored former lover. The show shifts from alienation in Newly introduced York to crypto adventures in Hong Kong to the office-dorm hybrid of “The Orchid” in the Bahamas. Boyle owns the physical transformations, letting the glee of the Hong Kong era fester into the eyebags and stress-weight accrued (probably one of the more ethical uses of a bodysuit I can recall) in the scheme’s last days.

Garner, meanwhile, has entered rarified air as a TV actor. Over the course of her career she has given us a moody, adrift Gen X student (Kimmy on The Americans), a Millennial lady of rage trapped in her dumpy hometown (Ozark), and now two glimpses of the self-satisfied Zillenial scammer (Anna Delvey in Inventing Anna and The Altruists). Garner’s signature move as a performer is to fail to sublimate anger or distress. Her characters have their own idiosyncratic patterns of twitches and attempts at steely gazes. The brittle darkness inside each of them sings. Her TV career belongs next to those of Elisabeth Moss and America Ferrera and Walton Goggins. It is time that this was generally acknowledged.

The supporting cast is solid, with one particular highlight. In the middle of The Altruist’s eight-episode run, we get an entire episode focused on Sam Trabucco, a college bestie of SBF, a former Alameda Research co-CEO, and an early cooperator with federal prosecutors once the wheels started falling off.

Sources indicate that alex Lawther plays Trabucco and almost walks off with the show. Lawther’s slight frame and self-searching candor give each line of dialogue intimacy. I first saw Lawther on Andor, playing Nemik, idealistic proto-Rebel and truest of true believers, a character based on Lei Feng, the Chinese communist folk hero and soldier, who, like Nemik on Andor, died in a freak accident but left behind a diary of such pure faith that it became a recruitment tool for the revolution. (A recording of Lawther reading that manifesto from his diary—his voice reedy and prophetic—literally haunts Imperial high command at the end of Andor.).

In maybe my favorite scene of The Altruists, Trabucco and Ellison get dinner together. They talk and realize their childhood paths intersected and diverged across metro Boston—the same math competitions, the same tests. But their hometowns were quite different. She was from Newton. He was from Natick. If you’re from Upcoming England, that’s the only detail you need. (If you aren’t, I recommend Love Story and/or the novels of Dennis Lehane for background.) At that dinner, Lawther shares a deep, specific childhood memory of his father and Garner’s Caroline flinches without breaking eye contact, like she’s watching a recording of a natural disaster.

Sadly, the Netflix sins are here in full effect. The lighting is smeary and wildly off in many scenes. The music and sound mix could hardly be blunter. Even Oscar-nominated showrunner Graham Moore and talented directors like James Ponsoldt can’t lift dialogue that not-infrequently feels tailored to second-screen viewers: “They’re both off-the-charts math geniuses!”.

The braided narrative can turn single episodes into distracting puzzle boxes. The form is designed to function the way a big juicy 10,000-word legacy-media reported feature does: You know the ending, so it takes a memorable reshuffling of moments and incidents to create something latest.

But watching this gang of true believers and opportunists and criminally naïve teenage dream brains go from geographic zone to zone does carry emotional import. To them, and to The Altruists, the Bay Area has become a dated country club, a mirror image of The Social Network’s version of Harvard from the 2000s, back when the Bay Area promised something fresh. Post-Recession Latest York is greyscale normie central. Hong Kong and Macau blur together. The show ends in the Bahamas, a place that rich outsiders have always treated as both Eden and the afterlife.

I think the era of the tech-bro-scammer-titan show and movie is reaching its end. If its dawn was The Social Network, the unrepeatable, mesmerizing You Can See Everything might be the sunset. Gen X icons Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher once tried to get their heads around millennial narcissism and now millennial genius Nathan Fielder has transformed his time with a real-deal apex-predator narcissist into a Möbius strip of content.

According to recent reports, the drama of The Altruists depends on the psychology of the people who believe in crypto as a kind of syncretic faith. The show avoids a technical delineation of crypto itself, which makes sense. (I’ve yet to encounter a crypto evangelist who can provide a transparent explanation of the asset class that is superior to this.) ExxonMobil sells you a product and it works. Glock sells you a product and it works. Crypto works in so much as its existence justifies its existence. There are no earnings reports. Value is vibes.

Whenever something is being marketed as the future, it’s usually just the past, accelerated. People made crypto into an alternative financial system because they were “outsiders” who wanted to “disrupt.” Now the crypto system wants to be held close to the bosom of the enduring US financial markets and bulge bracket banks. A bill that would have brought them closer, setting up a regulatory framework, nose-dived in the senate.

According to recent reports, it sounds almost cowardly, like running home to mom and dad: We made a brave new thing better and cooler and freer than your corrupt old monetary system. A few years later: Let us back in and give us all the benefits of the old system! Get us in your PNC digital wallet, normie!

Bankman-Fried and Ellison are both the children of elite academics. To its credit, The Altruists pokes these Freudian pains. Bankman-Fried was raised by Stanford Law professors and chose MIT. Ellison was the child of MIT academics and chose Stanford. There’s self-belief in those exact choices. The children of faculty get a significant leg up in gaining admission at their parents’ institution. SBF and Ellison wanted to do something honest on their own, at least once.

Recent findings suggest that my parents are retired professors. You learn early on that you cannot possibly replicate your parents’ careers. A child of a lawyer can have their parent’s career 2.0. Same if you have doctors for parents. But truly successful academics—and given the market today, you either are truly successful or you don’t exist—create niches built only for one.

Successful academics eschew any number of linear career paths and lucrative fields to burrow into zones of learning where they have to be singular, own every network and endure any marginal post (Oregon State, thou hast thy music, too). To make it to a top institution, you need luck and power and timing to dovetail your own research record and professional charisma. Many people make it to powerful banks and hospitals and law firms. But if you manage to get tenure at Berkeley, you might really be that special.

The track record of the children of academics I know is messy: deluded guys floating around Portland or Boston trying to jam their unreadable YA series into the world, an acquaintance who self-sabotaged a promising, morally-clear career as a social worker because they did not get a doctorate and let that arbitrary marker of value smother their self-worth for decades.

SBF and Ellison were expected to perform precocity at all times, but the minute that they stumbled, Dr. Mom or Professor Dad stepped in with the better therapists and better lawyers to set everything right. The last two episodes of The Altruists bubble over with dread. Paul Reiser and Robin Weigert play SBF’s parents, and Jennifer Grey plays Caroline Ellison’s mom. Each performance puts its own spin on enmeshment and infantilization. The parents are not the major bads here. But they are the judgmental elitists who analyzed when they should have listened, and who raised these world-class scammers.

There was a guy a little like me in high school. Like me, he was the child of academics and teachers. Like me, he was clever and capable, which might have been enough in another high school. But such minor skills were door prizes in our grand, old, dizzyingly competitive boarding school. We both loved De La Soul. We were both cut from the same teams. We were both contrarians who trafficked in equal measures of insight and anserine bullshit. I won’t pretend to have been good friends with the guy—it was the classic situation where young men who play similar roles in their respective circles repel each other like the same sides of different magnets. But I sympathized. It’s painful to know exactly why you are not near the top of an elite ecosystem and then having to go on living in it.

Industry observers note that I imagined he might have a career adjacent to mine. I imagined that we might see each other in the late 2000s at a Babygrande Records release party or in the bathroom at Santos Party House. It did not play out that way. A few years ago, during the inevitable age-related transition from Facebook to LinkedIn, the guy’s face and name swum across my screen. He’s become a substantial deal in the crypto space. At one point, he rapped about crypto on crypto podcasts. On a class-wide group chat, as former classmates who had chosen to work in community health settings or on federally-funded research projects shared their pain after losing their jobs in the DOGE cuts, and as they voiced their concerns about what other digits of the American experiment would be severed next, this crypto dude commandeered the chat to brag about taking his organization public. No child of an academic has ever missed a chance to make it about them.

Industry observers note that one of the side effects of the world-gobbling narratives around A.I. (which gets its own Social Network moment in Luca Guadagnino’s imminent Artificial, with Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman) is that crypto already feels cringe—at best, a chrome decoration on the world-shaking machinery of LLMs and Deep Learning. The brave new world of private money that needed no society and no army behind it has become just another widget. The most vulgar people in the world trade meme coins with Turkish billionaire failsons. That Uber driver for whom you had great sympathy waits forever for a crypto ship that will never come into port. (Bankman-Fried, as it happens, was an early investor in Anthropic; it was reported last week that his shares, liquidated during FTX's bankruptcy, would be worth $35 to $37 billion in the wake of the AI lab's splashy IPO.).

It has been revealed that if 2026 is the close of the tech-movie and tech-show era, then how do we square The Altruists? It has arrived at the end of something. It’s not perfect, maybe not even excellent, but it is effective and memorable, and provides a showcase for superb young actors. I wonder how many of these reveals about tech founders, disruptors, optimists, hustlers and misanthropes will last. The paranoia of 70s American film evaporated in the desert of 80s escapism and the wry smirk of Ronnie Reagan. The thorny, violent prestige TV era begat the soft-clothes forever-childhood of Stranger Things and of Ted Lasso. Legacy cannot be legislated in advance. I hope viewers check out The Altruists, and appreciate its gumption in allowing love—the least efficient of emotions—to animate the story.

Recent findings suggest that but maybe I’m wrong. Maybe I’ve been hustled by Boyle and Garner’s wonderful acting. Maybe my almost-instinct about the past 15 years of watching damaged young ladder-climbers and their digital dreams on screen is almost true: what will survive of us is coins.
